## Netcode audit — 2026-10-13

Audit requested by the human on 2026-10-13: what in the network code can cause freezes, lag, stutter or rubber-banding for a European user (about 200 ms of ping to Agni, simulators that lag now and then), and where Aurora can do better than Firestorm on the client side. Read: `crates/aurora-net` (circuit, session, capabilities, event queue, fetcher, object cache), the viewer side that drives it (`agent.rs`, `world/`, `scene/textures.rs`, `scene/meshes.rs`, `app.rs`, `ui/perf.rs`) and the matching Firestorm sources (`indra/llmessage`, `indra/llcorehttp`, `indra/newview`). Nothing here was measured on the grid by the audit: every figure marked "computed" is arithmetic from constants read in the code, and each item is one PR with its before / after measurement. The messages, capabilities and what the simulator expects do not change; only the client side does. A visible difference from Firestorm is said so in its item and is the human's decision.

- 🟡 Network adapters that lose their link under many downloads (issues [#1545](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1545), [#1546](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1546), PR [#1547](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1547) by a contributor, reworked at the human's request of 2026-10-30; task `aqtion-bounded-fetch`; validated by the human in demo with a simulated adapter on 2026-10-30): both reports are on a Marvell AQtion 10 Gbit adapter (Windows 11) that dropped until a reboot during login or a teleport, while the adaptive asset pace (`aurora-net/src/fetch_pace.rs`, 24 up to 192 requests) ran. Preferences › Network and cache › Download connections: Automatic (default), Follow the connection, Limited. Limited is the Legacy Viewer's bounded llcorehttp policy (`LLAppCoreHttp::init_data`): 24 requests at once, 32 kept connections per host. Automatic follows the connection. When an adapter whose description names AQtion or Aquantia is present (GetAdaptersAddresses at startup, `net_adapters.rs`), the downloads always stay limited (human request of 2026-10-30): Automatic and Limited both mean limited, "Follow the connection" is greyed with the reason on hover, and a "Follow the connection" saved before is applied as limited (logged once) without rewriting the saved choice; the row's hint names the adapter. Aurora keeps its adaptive pace as the default on purpose (a deliberate difference from the Legacy Viewer's fixed connections, item 21 of the netcode audit). Applies at the next launch; `AURORA_FETCH_SLOTS` still fixes the count to compare. Tests `adaptive_follows_the_link_and_limited_is_bounded`, `aqtion_and_aquantia_adapters_are_found_whatever_their_case`, `other_adapters_keep_the_adaptive_pace`, `without_the_adapter_each_choice_keeps_its_mode`, `with_the_adapter_every_choice_is_limited`, `follow_the_connection_is_blocked_only_with_an_adapter_known_to_drop`, `download_connections_stay_automatic_for_earlier_files`.
  - ⬜ Grid check by the reporters: login and teleports on the AQtion adapter (limited), then the adapter's driver updated.

> Today's grid logs (three sessions of 2026-10-13, RTX 4090, 500 to 1,500 fps): the `events` step costs 0.54 ms per frame at most on a one-second average, and the worst frames (0.4 to 1.5 s) are the first frame and waits outside the processor (`between`), not the network. But the logs hold no line about the network itself: no ping, loss, resend, queue age or input delay. Hence item 1 before anything else.

> Already better than Firestorm, to keep as it is: the network runs on its own runtime and is not tied to the frame rate (Firestorm reads the socket, flushes acks, resends and pings once per frame, with 20 ms or 400 messages per frame: `LLAppViewer::idleNetwork`, llappviewer.cpp); the UDP circuit and the seed capability start together at login (Firestorm waits for the capabilities and a decode loop before UseCircuitCode: llstartup.cpp STATE_SEED_CAP_GRANTED); cache misses are requested as each ObjectUpdateCached is read (Firestorm: once per frame); `Far` is sent in full on arrival (Firestorm: half the draw distance, then +10% per second: llviewermessage.cpp `send_agent_update`); downloads go through one priority queue with time-boxed results on the main thread (llcorehttp is first in, first out and its texture results are picked up by a sweep that takes 20 frames or more to go round: `LLViewerTextureList::updateImagesFetchTextures`); a disk cache hit never touches the network; our avatar's extrapolation tapers from 2 s to 3 s on a silent circuit (Firestorm hands `InterpolationTime` and `InterpolationPhaseOut` to the wrong setters, llviewerobjectlist.cpp `setPhaseOutUpdateInterpolationTime( interp_time )`: full speed for 3 s, then a dead stop).

Suggested order (1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13 and 15 are done): 17 and 19, then the rest; 3 and 4 are the ones that change what the user feels most and need the human's decision.

**Measure first**

- ✅ **1. Network line in the log and in the Performance window.** Nothing told how late an input leaves, how old an update is when it is applied, or how long the UDP loop stalls. Done: with `AURORA_PROFILE=1`, one `net summary` line per second of a grid session next to `perf summary` (`net_profile.rs`; fields in docs/TESTING.md, "Profiling › Network"): ping, last and smoothed; packets and throughput in / out; reliable packets resent, given up, duplicates, unacked; sequence numbers skipped by the simulators and packets that came late (their difference is what never arrived); longest time the session loop spent on one wake-up (`loop_max`); events applied by the main thread, most left waiting at the end of a frame and longest wait since the network sent them (each event now leaves the session with its time); AgentUpdates sent and longest delay between a change of the control flags and the AgentUpdate that carried it (`NetClient::set_controls`, not counted during a teleport); corrections of our avatar: simulator reports more than 0.5 m from the extrapolated position, like Firestorm's `AGENT_POSITION_SNAP`, and the largest distance, moves of more than 10 m left out; asset requests in flight, queued, finished, failed and retried, and one line per asset host with the HTTP version it answers in. Performance › Network shows the input delay (last one measured), the corrections of the session, the loop pause and the event wait of the last second, without the variable. Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_PERF=network` opens the window on that section (the demo has no circuit: the rows are there, their values empty). `check.ps1` green (1,818 tests passed, 23 ignored); unit tests of the counters, of the sequence gaps, of the corrections and of the line. Not counted: new HTTP connections (the HTTP client does not report them). Window and lines validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-13 ("Test net-summary").
  - First reference, Agni, 2026-10-13: one busy region, 92 s of walking, no teleport, medians of the `net summary` lines. Ping 202 ms (smoothed 234). Input delay 94 ms, 123 ms at the 95th percentile, 125 ms at most, over the 59 seconds that had a key change: what item 2 computed, and close to half the ping added on top of it. 6 corrections of our avatar, the largest 0.96 m. No resend, duplicate or sequence gap. Session loop: 0.11 ms, 3.8 ms on arrival (no cache write in so short a session: item 8 is not measured yet). Event wait 8 ms, 15 ms at the 95th percentile, the channel empty at the end of every frame. Both asset hosts answer in HTTP/1.1; 104 of the 637 asset requests failed, the ones listed in the log with a 403.

**Input latency and our own avatar**

- 🟡 **3. Movement prediction of our own avatar (visible difference from Firestorm: a choice in Preferences › Aurora › Movement, Firestorm's by default until the human has tried it on Agni, marked experimental meanwhile by a warning triangle and its tooltip).** Like Firestorm, Aurora moved our avatar only when the simulator's update came back (`LLViewerObject::processUpdateMessage`): at 200 ms of ping it started and stopped a fifth of a second after the key. Done (`own_motion.rs`, `agent.rs`, `app/own_motion.rs`): with "Instant", the drawn avatar is the simulator's extrapolated position plus a lead, the motion the keys asked for over the last delay (round trip + the simulator's step), which is what the simulator has not played yet since it plays our inputs that much later. The intent comes from the control flags actually sent (keys and autopilot), the body's heading and the run state; jumps and crouching on the spot are not predicted. The lead comes from the keys alone, so it cannot drift: once they are released it drains in one delay while the simulator plays the end of the motion. The drawn avatar glides to that aim (a critically damped follow of 0.08 s, about Firestorm's drawable damping), so a stop eases out over about 0.15 s instead of halting in one frame; after a release it only slows down (a simulator that stops a physics step later than the lead expected is caught up at the speed the avatar had), a simulator that stops a step sooner leaves the avatar where it is drawn, and a correction under 0.15 m at rest waits for the next move to fade (the human's demo trial of 2026-10-16 felt a jolt at each stop: the avatar halted in one frame, then moved 5 cm on or back when the simulator's stop arrived a frame apart from the lead's; measured before: 3.2 m/s lost in one frame and a 5 cm pop 200 ms later, 0.24 m of pull-back on the first stop; after: at most 0.5 m/s lost per 16 ms, no rise, no pull-back, at 60 and 500 fps). The walk goes on until the drawn avatar is under 0.5 m/s. When the simulator does not follow (a wall, a freeze, a push: its velocity under half the asked one once it should be moving), the lead fades (0.1 s half-life) and the server's motion alone is drawn until the keys change; three such failures within 10 s suspend it for 5 s. Never seated (on an object, a vehicle as passenger or driver, a prim at rest, the ground), during a teleport or before the arrival: a change of parent drops the lead and the first frame standing starts from the simulator's position. Seated, Firestorm's keys orbit the camera or go to the vehicle's script (`key_bindings.xml` <sitting>, `camera_move_forward_sitting`, llviewerinput.cpp): the flags still leave, the drawn avatar is where its seat carries it. On the land the lead follows the slope and stays in the known regions. The body turns with the drawn velocity. Calibration instead of step (a): the speeds per mode (walk, run, crouch, nudge, fly, climb), the ramps (start and stop) and the delay beyond the round trip are learned from the simulator's reports, seeded with walk 3.2, run 5.13, fly 16 m/s (crouch, nudge, climb, ramps and delay are guesses), and logged (`own motion learned: …`, `lead_max=` in `net summary`). Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_LINK=<ping>[,jitter=][,aurora|firestorm][,vehicle]` (`demo_link.rs`), a stand-in simulator behind a simulated link; with 200 ms and `AURORA_DEMO_KEY=up:pulse`: Firestorm's movement starts 250 to 317 ms after the press and stops 500 ms and 0.9 m after the release, Aurora's starts within one frame and stops within one frame, 0.00 to 0.01 m on (the same with 40 ms of jitter). `check.ps1` green; unit tests of the intent, the lead (round trip, wall, push, suspension, reset), the calibration, the seated cases (passenger, driver, prim at rest, ground, standing up) and the slow corrections. To verify on Agni, side by side with Firestorm's: walk, run, fly, stop and turn on flat land and on slopes; walking into a wall and being pushed; sitting on a vehicle and on a chair and standing up; a region crossing on foot; the `own motion learned` values (real speeds, ramps and delay) to replace the guesses. The default is the human's choice once tried.
- 🟡 **4. Softer corrections of our avatar and its animations with the keys (visible difference from Firestorm, with 3).** With Aurora's movement, a correction of 0.5 to 3 m fades with a 0.25 s half-life instead of Firestorm's 0.06 s (`OBJECT_DAMPING_TIME`, `LLDrawable::updateXform`), beyond 3 m with 0.06 s, beyond 10 m it snaps as before; the gap rides on the extrapolation instead of the drawable chasing the moving position (as `world/motion.rs` already does for the other objects), so a walking avatar is not drawn late, and the camera follows the drawn position. The corrections above 0.5 m are still counted (`AGENT_POSITION_SNAP`). Checked: Firestorm starts our walk, run and fly only on the simulator's AvatarAnimation (`process_avatar_animation`, llviewermessage.cpp; `LLVOAvatar::processAnimationStateChanges`). With Aurora's movement they start with the key and stop with its release (`own_motion::Locomotion`): the simulator's stock motion the keys will bring (walk, run, crouchwalk, fly, hover up / down) replaces the stand at once, the simulator's signal takes over keeping the cycle's start, and on a release the moving motions are hidden until the simulator stops them (a stand or a hover in their place); a start or stop the simulator does not confirm within the round trip + 0.6 s is dropped. The AO sees the same signals, so its overrides follow the keys too. Firestorm's movement: everything as before (the setting off, or offline without the simulated link). To verify on Agni with 3: no foot sliding at a stop, no double start of the walk, the AO's walk and stand following.

Now the local stop is kept past that wait while the simulator does not report our avatar moving, 3 s at most (`Locomotion::overlay`, `HOLD`); a report of motion (pushed, a key lost) gives the simulator's walk back after the wait as before. The same for a start: the local walk is kept past the wait while the drawn avatar moves (it stopped under a moving avatar, feet sliding, when the simulator's walk signal was late). Reproduced in demo with `AURORA_DEMO_LINK=350,aurora,trace,stoplag=800` (new: the stand-in keeps its walk signal that long once stopped) and `AURORA_DEMO_KEY=up:pulse`: the walk came back 1.1 s after each release; now none, with `stoplag=800` or `1500`. ⬜ To verify on Agni: stops with an AO, in a busy region.

The rule now holds horizontally and for the last 0.5 m of a stop only; the height always glides to the simulator's (fall, landing, take-off), and a correction left at rest waits for the next move horizontally only (a landing left the feet 0.14 m in the ground). Grid trace: `AURORA_OWN_MOTION_TRACE=1` (new, docs/TESTING.md). Unit test of the Agni case (hovering, no key, a 5.8 m fall): 5.9 m hung before, now the glide's 0.8 m behind at 10 m/s and on the ground at the end. ⬜ To verify on Agni: stop flying at rest and while moving, jump, walk off a ledge.

Scale the lead's motion by the main region's dilation (`SimulatorMotion::time_dilation`), keep the calibration in simulator time (the reports' velocities), and write the dilation in `net summary` and the `AURORA_OWN_MOTION_TRACE` line; verify on Agni in a busy region (an event, a crowded club). **Other avatars and moving objects**

- ✅ **5. Extrapolation and smoothing of the others (alignment with Firestorm, then better).** Everything that is not our avatar was drawn by `Object::predicted`: position + velocity × time, with the time cut at 0.6 s, no time dilation, and each update applied as it is. An avatar or a vehicle on a steady course froze 0.6 s after its last update, although the simulator deliberately sends nothing while the object follows the path it announced (`LLViewerObject::interpolateLinearMotion`), then jumped at the next one; a spinning object (llTargetOmega) stopped for good after 0.6 s; every correction was a snap. Fixed (`world/motion.rs`): an object follows its reported velocity, acceleration and spin for as long as the circuit of its region lives, with Firestorm's physics step (the closed form of its per-frame sum, the same at any frame rate; the angle of a spin keeps its precision for days). Time is the simulator's: each region has a clock (`ObjectStore::motion_time`, advanced by `World::advance_motion` from the dilation and the last packet of every simulator, `NetStats::simulators`) that runs at the region's time dilation, slows down after 2 s of silence of its circuit and stops at 3 s; an object then stays where it was and goes on when the circuit is back. A report that puts an object elsewhere than where it was drawn opens a gap that fades with Firestorm's half-life of 0.06 s, in position and rotation, snapping beyond 10 m (`Correction`, the damping of `LLDrawable::updateXform`); while it fades the object counts as moving for the scene, then is placed for good. Not corrected: a new object, a change of parent (sitting, standing up), an object that came from another region, and a pose written locally since the report (a drag in the build tools). An extrapolated avatar stays half its height above the land. **Better than Firestorm, deliberately:** the fading also applies to objects in motion (Firestorm only damps avatars and objects whose velocity is zero, `LLViewerObject::updateDrawable`, so its physical objects and vehicles snap), and it rides on the extrapolation instead of chasing it, so a moving object is not drawn late. `check.ps1` green (1,863 tests passed, 23 ignored); tests of the extrapolation (steady course, sum of Firestorm's steps at 10 / 45 / 600 frames a second, spin over days), of the clock, of the correction (half-life, shortest turn, too small / too far) and of the store (clock per region, border crossing, fading and its end, local write, change of parent). Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-13 ("Test others-motion", 206 s, two regions, one teleport): walking avatars, vehicles and physical objects, spinning objects, scripted doors, build tools drag, sitting and standing up, nothing to report; `sync` 0.10 ms per frame at the median, 0.27 at the 95th percentile.
  - ⬜ Later: stop an extrapolated object at the edge of a region that has no neighbour there (Firestorm's clip in `interpolateLinearMotion`; our avatar already has it, `clip_to_visible_regions`), and a demo scenario with sparse updates once the simulated link of item 1 exists.
- 🟡 **6. Update times taken at reception.** `update_time` and `last_server` were `Instant::now()` when the main thread applied the event, after its wait in the event channel (Firestorm takes the frame time too: `mLastInterpUpdateSecs`), so every update shifted a moving object by speed × wait. Done: each event already left the session with the time it was sent, right after the datagram was read and decoded; `World::apply_received` hands it to the object updates: with Aurora's movement our avatar's report starts its extrapolation from that moment (`AgentState::on_server_update_at`; with Firestorm's movement it keeps the frame time, as on Firestorm and before), and an object's motion is stamped on its region's clock at that moment (`ObjectStore::report_clock`: the clock, plus or minus the time from its last tick at the region's rate), its correction measured against where it was drawn for that moment. Events applied without a time (the demo, the tests) keep the clock as it is. The objects and the other avatars take the reading time whatever the movement setting: it extends item 5, which is already outside the toggle and deliberately better than Firestorm. Tests of the stamping (before and after the tick, time dilation). To verify on Agni: other avatars walking and vehicles driving past look as smooth as before or smoother, with no shift at each update in a busy region. Later, to decide with the measurements of item 1: compensation by half the ping (Firestorm's `PingInterpolate`, off by default) or a short interpolation buffer for the other avatars.

**UDP circuit when the link or the simulator lags**

- 🟡 **8. No file work on the session loop.** The object cache of a region was read in the RegionHandshake handler, and every changed cache was serialised and written every 120 s, when its simulator went and at the end, all on the task that reads the socket: during that time nothing was received, acknowledged or answered. Measured on this PC (default profile, SSD, file already in the system's cache): 3.3 ms to read and 3.1 ms to write a cache of 12,827 objects (3.9 MiB), 13.8 and 13.1 ms for a full one of 60,000 (18 MiB), for each region — up to nine in the same tick — and more on a cold or slow disk. Done (`session/object_cache.rs`, `objcache.rs`): the file is read by a blocking task and RegionHandshakeReply leaves when it is loaded, with the same flags as before (its "cache empty" bit needs the cache); a handshake sent again meanwhile does not read twice, a simulator that left gets nothing. The payloads are shared, so the loop only takes a snapshot of a cache that changed (0.15 ms for 12,827 objects, 1.1 ms for 60,000) and one writer writes the snapshots in the order they were taken: two writes of one region never overlap and the latest wins. A write that failed is taken again at the next period; the end of the session waits for the writer, so that the next one reads up-to-date files; clearing the cache in Preferences also drops what was being read or waited for the writer. Firestorm reads the cache on its main thread, in the same handler (`LLViewerRegion::unpackRegionHandshake` → `loadObjectCache`). Log, without any variable: `object cache for <region>: … entries, read in … ms` and `object cache written: … objects, … KiB in … ms`. Tests: content and order of the snapshots, failed write, reply to the handshake held until the cache is read (cached region, new region, no region id, repeated handshake, simulator gone), writes in order and read back, cleared cache. `check.ps1` green (1,870 tests passed, 24 ignored). Human trial on Agni on 2026-10-13 ("Test udp-buffers-cache-io", 213 s with a teleport there and back, then a new login of 66 s): objects appear as before on login, after both teleports and after the new login, which read the file the first session wrote at its end; four reads of about 12,800 objects in 3.1 to 4.0 ms, the reply to the handshake leaving 3 to 4 ms after it; one periodic write and one at the end, 3.1 and 3.3 ms; `loop_max` stays under 0.45 ms during both logins (5 to 6 ms in the second of the handshake before).
  - ⬜ To verify on Agni: an arrival in a region that has neighbours (several caches read at once, the cache of a neighbour written when it is left: both regions of the trial stood alone), and Preferences › clear the cache during a session.
  - ⬜ Later: the loop still pauses 5 to 21 ms now and then during the six seconds that follow a teleport (both teleports of the trial, neither login), in seconds where the main thread also runs frames of 50 to 70 ms. It is not file work, and not the decoding of cache hits (1 µs per object, measured on a local cache of 12,955 objects). To find out: name in `net summary` which wake-up held the loop (datagram, tick, command, capability) and whether its thread was working or waiting for a processor while the decode workers take every core.
- 🟡 **9. Seed capability: a failure must not be final.** `resolve_seed` tries 4 times in about 5 s, then the viewer shows "capabilities unavailable" and never asks again (`caps_requested` stays set in `request_caps` / `on_caps`): on a simulator that lags at the wrong moment the region stays without textures, inventory or teleports until a relog. Firestorm tries 30 times (`MAX_CAP_REQUEST_ATTEMPTS`, llviewerregion.cpp). Capability requests also have no overall timeout (`caps_http` only has a connection timeout): one that hangs never returns. To do: retries up to Firestorm's count with a capped delay and some jitter, a timeout on every capability request, the alert only when everything failed, and a new attempt on the next region change. **Done on 2026-10-13** (`caps::resolve_seed`, `SeedRetry::FIRESTORM`): the seed is asked 31 times like `LLViewerRegionImpl::requestBaseCapabilitiesCoro` (more than `MAX_CAP_REQUEST_ATTEMPTS` failures give the region up), each request given the 30 s of llcorehttp, the next one 1, 2, 4 then 5 s later (its `HTTP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MIN` / `MAX_DEFAULT`) with up to a fifth more at random; a reply that is not a map counts as a failure, as Firestorm's "malformed response". The requests stop when the session ends; one request per simulator, a new seed takes the place of the old and the answer to a previous seed is ignored (`mHttpResponderID`). The alert comes only once every attempt failed, for the agent's region, and the seed is asked again when that region is entered again. Six tests (spacing, a seed that answers at the fourth request, one given up after every attempt or when no longer wanted, a request left without reply, the session's handling of a stale answer and of a failure). Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-13 for the ordinary case: a login and a teleport, 54 capabilities each time at the first request, 0.3 s after the arrival. 🟡 because the retries themselves cannot be provoked on the grid: the log says `seed capability answered at attempt n` when they served.
  - ⬜ Later: a timeout on the other capability requests (`caps::request_llsd` has none; the event queue has its own).
- 🟡 **10. Event queue kept alive in a quiet place, errors like Firestorm.** The failure counter of the loop was only reset by a reply that carried events, and a long poll that ends without one is cut as a transport error about once a minute ("event queue error: error sending request", present in every grid log). In a place where nothing happens the errors added up, and at the 21st the loop gave up for good ("event queue for … giving up", seen in the log of a long session of 2026-10-09 after twenty-odd minutes of errors a minute apart): from then on no TeleportFinish, no chat session, no parcel event reached the viewer until a relog. Statuses 499 to 504 were also polled again after 100 ms whatever the time the request took, without counting: a simulator answering an error at once received 10 requests per second. Fixed like `LLEventPollImpl::eventPollCoro` (lleventpoll.cpp; `after_poll` in `caps.rs`): a poll the simulator held 10 s or more (`MIN_SECONDS_PASSED`) and that ended without an event is "no event" and forgets the errors, whatever ended it — our timeout, a 499 / 500 / 502 / 503 / 504, or the held connection being cut, which is how that end shows through our HTTP client; anything sooner, and any other status, is an error: wait 1 s + 3 s per error already counted, give up after 15 in a row (about 5 minutes of continuous failure); a 404 closes the queue. A reply without an id keeps the previous acknowledgement. When the queue of the agent's region gives up, the session ends with the "connection lost" message, as Firestorm's forced disconnect, instead of staying open without teleports; a neighbour only loses its own events (warning in the log). `net summary` gains `event_queue idle= errors=` (docs/TESTING.md). `check.ps1` green; tests of the rule (a quiet place for hours, back-off and give-up, recovery, closed queue), of the loop against a local server (events, acknowledgements across an error) and of the lost queue (agent's region, neighbour, queue replaced since). Unchanged: our 75 s timeout (Firestorm: 30 s). Human trial on Agni on 2026-10-13 ("Test event-queue-errors"): 5 min 25 s alone in a skybox, 10 idle polls (two a minute), no error, where the previous code counted one about once a minute.
  - ⬜ To verify on Agni: a teleport after a quiet stay of more than twenty minutes (the session above had no teleport and stopped before the old limit); nothing on the grid can exercise the give-up and its disconnection on demand.
- 🟡 **11. Bandwidth asked from the simulator (Firestorm's rule, a higher default).** `send_complete_agent_movement` sent fixed throttles: 1,788 kb/s in all, 800 of them for the objects (the Task channel), whatever the link. A simulator never sends faster than what it is asked, and on an arrival it sent just that: this is what an arrival in a region that is not in the object cache waits for, and what the avatars wait for as clouds, since what they wear is never cached. Done, port of LLViewerThrottle (`aurora-net/src/throttle.rs`): the setting is Firestorm's `ThrottleBandwidthKBPS` (Preferences › Network and cache › Maximum bandwidth, by steps of 50 as its slider; `bw <kbps>` in the chat, which only said it could not); it is shared between the seven channels along Firestorm's four presets, interpolated and, beyond 1,000, extrapolated from the last two; a session first asks for one and a half times the setting, 6,000 kb/s at most; every 5 s a tenth of the setting less is asked when more than 3 % of the packets were lost or the viewer is 256 packets behind, a tenth more when less than 0.5 % were lost and it is not, between a fifth of the setting and one and a half times; a change goes to the agent's simulator, and an arrival sends what is asked then. The packets lost are the sequence numbers the simulators skipped and never filled (item 1); the backlog is the events the main thread has not applied, where Firestorm counts the packets its frame has not read (`LLPacketRing::getBufferLoadRate`). `simulator bandwidth:` lines in the log tell what is asked at first and at each change; `AURORA_BANDWIDTH_KBPS=<n>` sets it for a launch without changing the Preferences (docs/TESTING.md). **Different from Firestorm, decided by the human on the measurements below:** the default is 4,000 instead of 3,000, and the slider goes up to it instead of stopping at 3,000: 6,000 kb/s asked instead of 4,500, of which 2,050 for the objects instead of 1,528, the most Firestorm's own code ever asks (its debug setting reaches it). Measured on Agni by the human on 2026-10-13 ("Test sim-throttle"), arrivals by teleport in busy regions that were not in the cache, a different region each time, same link, the 60 s that follow: before, 596 to 648 kb/s received at the median, 200 to 220 objects a second, avatars shown after 35 and 43 s at the median, 17 and 18 of them only at the 60 s limit of their loading; with Firestorm's default, 1,531 kb/s (the 1,528 asked for the objects), about 530 objects a second, avatars after 21.8 s at the median and 44.7 s at most, none at the limit out of 59, 0.47 % of the packets lost; with 4,000, 2,475 kb/s, about 590 objects a second and the region complete in less than 40 s, avatars after 10.1 s at the median and 22.9 s at most, none at the limit out of 39, 0.07 % lost. The main thread never fell behind (two events left at the end of a frame at most), and what was asked never had to be lowered. The slider moved during a session sent each new value to the simulator (log). `check.ps1` green (1,895 tests passed, 24 ignored); tests: the groups against Firestorm's figures, the first request, the steps down and up and their bounds, the share lost from the counters, the `bw` command.
  - ⬜ To verify on Agni: the `bw` command in a session; and, when a link allows it, what happens with losses (the trial never lost enough for the request to be lowered: that rule is tested by unit tests only).

An experiment build where a variable lifted that ceiling, 15,000 kb/s asked of which 5,182 for the objects, two arrivals in busy regions that were not in the cache (Agni, 2026-10-13, "Test throttle-ceiling", the same link as the trials above, a 5G one): the simulators sent no more than with 6,000. **Loading: assets**

- ✅ **13. HTTP/2 for the assets, and concurrency that adapts: measured, nothing to change.** The audit computed a ceiling of about 120 asset requests a second (24 connections, one request each, 200 ms a round trip) and proposed HTTP/2 and a number of requests in flight that adapts. Both were measured on Agni by the human on 2026-10-13, and neither holds. (a) The asset hosts do not speak HTTP/2: with `reqwest` built with its `http2` feature and the asset client offering it ("Test asset-http2", the login and the capabilities kept on HTTP/1.1 as Firestorm's llcorehttp), both hosts, the textures' and the bakes', still `answer in HTTP/1.1`. The feature was not kept. Firestorm only tries HTTP/2 behind a test variable too (`_httpoprequest.cpp`: `getenv("VIEWERASSET")`). (b) The 24 requests at a time are rarely the limit: a request to the asset hosts is answered much faster than the simulator's 200 ms: the fetcher finished up to 338 and 400 requests in a second in the two sessions, 60 to 70 ms each with 24 at a time. Over two arrivals in busy regions that were not in the cache ("Test texture-first-pixels", 216 s, 22,899 replies): 116 replies a second at the median, 217 at the 90th percentile; 155 of the 195 seconds with downloads ended with free slots and nothing waiting; all 24 slots were taken at the end of 40 s; more than 100 requests waited in 5 s, 210 at most. What an arrival waits for is the simulator sending its objects (about 210 a second for more than a minute, see item 11), then the decodes. The figures of the demo of item 15 (`net=200`) are therefore those of a slow link, not of this one.
  - ⬜ To take again only on evidence: a link where the requests do wait (the `queued=` of `net summary` staying in the hundreds), or asset hosts that answer in HTTP/2 one day (the line `asset host … answers in` tells; the client must be built with `http2` to see it).
- 🟡 **14. Requests that follow what is wanted: cancel and re-prioritise.** A request kept the priority it had when it was queued and nothing was ever cancelled: after a camera turn or a teleport, what was no longer wanted kept its place in front of what is on screen. Done (`aurora-net/src/fetch.rs`, `scene/fetch_priority.rs`): the fetcher's queue (`FetchQueue`) takes a new rank for a request still waiting (`Fetcher::reprioritise`) and drops one (`Fetcher::cancel`); once sent, a request runs to its end and its result is ignored, as Firestorm never cancels one in flight. A texture waiting for a slot is ranked again at each pass of `recompute_wants` when its size on screen moved by half (`fetch_priority::changed`), and dropped when nothing uses it any more (a region left, an object gone: Firestorm clears every texture request at a teleport, `LLViewerTextureList::updateImages`); a mesh follows its nearest user (`MeshStreamer::need`, the size on screen of the object, radius over distance as Firestorm's `calculate_score` in llmeshrepository.cpp) and its waiting download goes when the scene lets its last geometry go (`MeshStreamer::unwant`, Firestorm drops the pending requests whose volumes are gone). - ✅ **15. One round trip to the first pixels.** The first request of a texture was a fixed 16 KiB (`INITIAL_BYTES`); when that was not enough for the wanted level, the data was not decoded and a second range was asked: two round trips and the queue before anything but grey. It also left before the size of the texture on screen was known (that size was noted when the turn of its object came, up to 30 frames later): at the same rank as every other texture, and its level computed for a file of 512 pixels until the next pass, one level too fine for a 1024 texture (four times the pixels decoded, four times the bytes asked). Firestorm also takes two steps (600 bytes, then the range of the level: `FIRST_PACKET_SIZE`, LLTextureFetchWorker::doWork). Done (`scene/textures.rs`): (a) an object whose faces were just built has the size of its textures on screen noted in the same frame (`Scene::fresh_usage`), so the first request of a texture in view leaves at the rank that size gives it; (b) that request asks what a 1024 texture needs to show that many pixels (`first_bytes`: 16 KiB up to 128 pixels, 44.6 KiB up to 256, 172.6 KiB beyond, never the whole file before its size is known), so one reply is enough for most; (c) when the file tells its size, from the first bytes or from the disk cache, the level wanted is computed again for that size (`Entry::want_for_its_size`); (d) when the bytes held still do not reach the level wanted but hold a coarser one, that one is decoded and shown while the rest is asked (`Entry::holds_first_pixels`). **Better than Firestorm, deliberately:** it shows nothing of a texture before its second reply. Measured in demo, 400 textures of a local cache downloaded from a local server at 200 ms a request (`AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=400,400,j2k=<folder>,net=200,size=3`), three alternated passes of the previous and the new behaviour in one binary: wait before the first pixels, weighted by the size on screen, 2.30 to 2.46 s → 0.73 to 0.75 s (2.25 → 1.83 s unweighted); requests 490 to 497 → 408; bytes 9.1 to 9.4 MB → 6.2 MB; pixels decoded 6.0 to 6.3 Mpx → 3.4 Mpx; every texture shown after 4.26 s → 3.46 to 3.96 s. What remains is the ceiling of 24 requests at a time (item 13). The `texture load:` line gains the wait before the first pixels of the downloaded textures, plain and weighted by their size on screen, and the first requests sent for a texture not seen yet. Demo: `net=<ms>` downloads the files of `j2k=` from a local asset server (`demo_asset_server.rs`) that answers after that delay, `size=<m>` makes the objects larger on screen (docs/TESTING.md); this is the simulated link for the assets, to reuse for items 13, 14 and 16. Tests: first range, level held by the bytes, first pixels, level for the size of the file, the pass keeping the size it saw, the asset server (requests, ranges, several requests on one connection). `check.ps1` green (1,885 tests passed, 24 ignored). Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-13 ("Test texture-first-pixels", 231 s: a login in a region in the cache, then two teleports to busy regions never visited), nothing to report on screen. In the log, the two arrivals without a cache downloaded 5,508 and 5,621 textures: first pixels 0.30 and 0.17 s after their request on average, 0.16 and 0.11 s weighted by their size on screen; 1.22 and 1.32 replies per texture downloaded; 3,353 and 1,774 first requests for textures not in view. No figure from before on the grid: the measure is new.
  - 🟡 Done with item 14: a new texture starts at its coarsest level (`MAX_DISCARD_LEVEL`), the one `recompute_wants` gives whatever is out of view, instead of a quarter of its size; what is in view has its size noted before its first read (`want_before_the_first_pass`). Turning the camera shows a texture seen for the first time at its coarsest level first, as it already did for every texture after the first pass. In the arrival demo without a turn, decode CPU 2.9 → 2.4 s for the same pixels; to read on Agni: the decodes of the first 10 s of a login (2,208 of 3,590 at `want: 2` before).
- 🟡 **16. Priorities between kinds of assets.** Every mesh was queued at 1e12, settings and landmarks at 1e12, materials and sounds at 9e11, animations at 8e11, textures at 1e5 at most plus their size on screen: on arrival the animations of the avatars, our own bakes and the sky waited for the whole mesh queue, far meshes included. Done (`aurora_net::Lane`, `scene/fetch_priority.rs`): two lanes. The urgent one goes first, ranked by kind: sky and water settings and a landmark a window waits on, then our own bakes (`/texture/<our agent>/` in the bake URL, Firestorm's `BOOST_AVATAR_BAKED_SELF`), interface images and what we wear (meshes worn by our avatar, HUDs), then animations, sounds, PBR materials. The bulk lane holds meshes and textures ranked together by their size on screen in pixels, what shows nothing yet first, a mesh before a texture of the same size (without its mesh an object is not there at all). Firestorm gives each kind its own connections (`LLAppCoreHttp::init_data`, llappcorehttp.cpp); here the lanes share the 24 slots: 4 kept for the urgent lane were tried and left out, since once its few requests were served they stayed idle and slowed the whole arrival by a sixth (15.1 → 17.5 s); an urgent request waits for the next slot to free up, a few milliseconds. Measured in demo with the new `AURORA_DEMO_ARRIVAL` (an arrival in a busy region: 1,200 objects all around, one in three a mesh, 16 avatars playing 32 animations, every asset downloaded from the local asset server, the avatar turning round after 3 s), alternated passes of `main` and the branch in one session: the 32 animations arrived after 0.67 s instead of 4.08 (200 ms a request), 0.25 s instead of 0.52 to 0.58 (70 ms).
- 🟡 **17. Meshes: only what is drawn, and nothing heavy on the main thread.** A mesh was downloaded whole, every level of detail and its physics, in one request, and the main thread copied the whole body, parsed the header and inflated the skin when it arrived. Done (`scene/meshes.rs`, `scene/mesh_bytes.rs`), port of LLMeshRepoThread's requests (`fetchMeshHeader`, `fetchMeshLOD`, `fetchMeshSkinInfo`, llmeshrepository.cpp): the start of the asset first, then only the blocks drawn (the level of detail, `actual_lod`, and the skin) by byte ranges, two blocks less than 4 KiB apart in one request; a finer level wanted later is asked then. **Different from Firestorm, deliberately:** the first request is sized by the finest level wanted, 8 KiB for the two coarsest, 32 KiB for the medium one, the whole asset for the high one (Firestorm: 4 KiB, then the block). Measured on a local set of 3,000 mesh assets: their blocks go from the coarsest level to the finest, then the physics and the skin, and the high level is three quarters of the bytes; to show the lowest, low or medium level this takes 1.24, 1.33 and 1.35 requests for 6, 8 and 32 % of the bytes of the whole assets, and splitting the high level would take 1.86 requests for 80 % (one more round trip for what is near, for a fifth of its bytes). The bytes are parsed by jobs (header, skin, `MeshArrival`): the main thread keeps them without copying. What is held goes to the disk cache as parts (`AMSH`), a whole asset as it is, so older cache files stay valid; media picking, the hover estimate of rigged shoes and the shape editor's preview read the finest level held (`MeshView::lod_section`) instead of the cache file or the whole asset. Measured with `AURORA_DEMO_ARRIVAL`, whose asset server gained a shared bandwidth (`bw=<Mb/s>`): a heavy arrival on a link held by its bytes (3,000 objects, `net=70,bw=100`, as the link of the Agni trial of item 14), half of what is in front shown after 7.3 s instead of 9.2, nine tenths after 9.3 instead of 11.2, everything after 15.5 instead of 17.4, mesh bytes 49.7 MB instead of 85.8; a busy place on the same link (the same arrival with 30 avatars wearing 6 rigged meshes each, `avatars=30,worn=6`), half of what is in front after 10.0 s instead of 11.9, nine tenths of what the avatars wear after 10.9 s instead of 12.5, everything after 19.1 instead of 20.9, mesh bytes 76.7 MB instead of 112.6; with only the round trip as the limit (`net=200`, no bandwidth), about the same (nine tenths of what is in front 8.5 s instead of 8.1, everything 14.9 instead of 14.75; 467 mesh requests instead of 400, 20.8 MB instead of 34.0). `check.ps1` green. Tried by the human on Agni on 2026-10-16 with the mesh cache set aside (textures and objects kept): a login then a teleport to a busy region, a camera turn, coming near far meshes, a teleport away and back. 15,258 meshes loaded, none failed; in the busy region the 6,430 meshes not yet held arrived within 30 s of the teleport (278 MB); for the 13,708 meshes also held before the trial the parts kept weigh 292 MB against 1,729 MB for the whole assets (17 %); back in that region everything was there again with 0.9 MB downloaded (the parts on disk are read back), finer levels were fetched as the camera came near (153 MB). ⬜ To verify on Agni: rigged meshes worn in a crowd at their finest level, the shape editor's preview and media on a mesh face.
  - 🟡 A mesh cache file is never replaced by less (`MeshBytes::save`): each write keeps what the file already holds, so a whole asset stays whole when a few of its blocks are written after a read of it that failed, and the blocks of a later write are kept when an earlier write, with fewer of them, finishes after it (the writes are jobs; one at a time now). The tests' streamers have no disk cache (an empty folder): they ran in the crate's folder and wrote `crates/aurora-viewer/mesh/<id>.mesh`, one of which had been committed; it is removed and those folders are ignored. Unit test: a whole file stays whole, an earlier write does not drop a later one's block (fails with the plain write).

- ⬜ **18. Failures that end for good, and one that never ends.** A mesh, an animation or a sound that failed 4 times is abandoned for the session (`scene/meshes.rs`, `scene/anim.rs`, `scene/sounds.rs`): an outage of the asset servers leaves invisible meshes and missing animations until a relog (Firestorm also gives up on a mesh level after its HTTP retries). A texture that does not decode is dropped and downloaded again about every 6 s, forever, because the download resets the failure counter (`TextureStreamer::on_fetch`). To do: a delay that grows to a ceiling without a final state for anything but a 404, reset on a region change; a separate counter of decode failures with a long retry.

Done (`TextureStreamer::update`): the textures ready for a decode are gathered while the list is walked and the free slots go to the most urgent, ranked as the uploads are (`UploadPriority`: what shows nothing yet, then the largest on screen). Measured with items 14 and 16 (see above).

**Loading: arrival in a region, and frame times**

- ⬜ **21. A region that comes back in reach is applied in one frame.** Returning to a region left less than a minute ago puts back all its objects and replays every event received meanwhile inside a single call (`World::unpark_region`, `world/parked.rs`), outside the time box of the events; parking does the same in the other direction. To do: both spread over frames like the rest of the arrivals (the nearest objects first); measure the worst frame on a teleport there and back.
- ⬜ **22. Network events: two lanes and a budget tied to the frame.** The main thread applies the events of the network in arrival order for 8 ms per frame at most (`App::frame`, "network events (time-boxed)"). On this PC the box is far from full; on a slower one or in a dense arrival, 8 ms is more than a whole frame at 165 Hz, and the position of our avatar, the chat and the teleport messages wait behind thousands of object updates. To do, after the queue age of item 1 shows it happens: what is small and urgent (updates of avatars, removals, teleport, chat) ahead of the bulk (full updates, cache hits) while keeping the order of the messages of one object, and a budget that is a share of the frame time. Firestorm: 20 ms or 400 messages per frame for everything, in order.
- ⬜ **23. Performance window: a graph that shows hitches rather than noise.** The graph draws the raw rate of each of the last 240 frames (`ui/perf.rs` `graph`): at several hundred frames per second a variation of half a millisecond moves the line by hundreds of images per second, so it saws even when nothing is felt. To do: a line smoothed over a short window with the worst frame of each window drawn apart (what the eye feels), the choice of frame time in milliseconds, and the marks of item 1 (corrections, pauses of the network loop) on the same time axis. The true periodic spike already listed in "Optimisation" (`recompute_wants`, one frame in thirty) stays there.
  - 🟡 Spikes above the frame rate cap at each click and mouse move (human report, 2026-10-16): the graph took each frame's time from the start of the frame, after the input events of the loop, while the frame limiter paces from its own end. A click or a mouse move handled before one frame and not the next made that one look a few milliseconds shorter (2 ms at a cap of 160 reads as 235 frames per second), though the frames left evenly (`perf summary` showed no frame under the cap's period). The graph now takes the time from one end of the limiter to the next (`App::frame`, `paced`); the time step of the frame and `perf summary` are unchanged. Validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-16, side by side with the old build: clicks and mouse moves no longer spike.

- 🟡 Alpha under the water drawn before the water ([#1678](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1678); human request, 2026-11-01, task `underwater-alpha`): while the camera is above the water, the blended faces whose bounds reach below the agent region's water height are drawn before the water and the scene copy it refracts, back to front, rigged first, writing depth from 1/255 (also into the single-sampled depth the water samples, with MSAA), without glow, like the Legacy Viewer's POOL_ALPHA_PRE_WATER (LLDrawPoolAlpha::renderPostDeferred, lldrawpoolalpha.cpp); a face crossing the surface is in both lists, each draw clipped to its side (waterClip, deferredUtil.glsl), at the flat region water height the lists are split at (LLEnvironment::getWaterHeight for both), not enhanced water's displaced level; the glow of a blended face crossing the surface clipped the same way; portal surfaces stay whole after the water, ban lines are clipped to the camera's side (the Legacy Viewer draws them behind the water's depth). The faces under the water also go into the click picking, the occlusion and contact-shadow depth, the wireframe view and the triangle count. The water's refraction and fog then cover them instead of their being drawn crisp over the surface. Under the water nothing changes. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_WATER=…:alpha`. GPU 2.20 → 2.12 ms (noise) on the demo scene, MSAA 4×. Validated by the human on the grid on 2026-11-01; re-check of the review's fixes pending (the list under the water was not copied into the frame packet: the faces wholly under it were not drawn).
  - ⬜ later: with the camera under the water, the Legacy Viewer swaps the two sides (the alpha above the surface goes before the water seen from below); Aurora keeps its previous order there.
  - ⬜ later: particles under the water drawn before it too (the Legacy Viewer's particles are alpha groups).
- 🟡 GPU stall when a graphics setting rebuilds the pipelines ([#1746](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1746), [#1722](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1722); task `async-pipeline-rebuild`, 2026-10-31; [PR #1755](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1755); validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-31, AA and SSR switches without a hitch; to check by QA on AMD and Intel): changing the MSAA samples or SSR rebuilt every render pipeline on the render thread in the middle of a frame (`apply_settings` → `make_pipelines`), with no pipeline cache; AMD (amdvlk, 9 s) and Intel (Arc B580, 36 s) drivers took long enough for the viewer to report a GPU stall. The set (scene and impostor pipelines) is now compiled on a worker thread (`PipelineBuild` in renderer.rs); the frames keep their samples and SSR meanwhile, the other settings applying at once, and take the new pipelines with their targets on the frame the set arrives. A newer request drops a set still compiling. `RenderStats::settings` / `Renderer::settings_applied` tell the main thread when the frames have the settings asked: the photo quality's photo (MSAA 8x) and `AURORA_CAPTURE` wait for it. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_AA_SWITCH`. Measured on an RTX 5070 (demo, MSAA 4x → 8x → 2x → 4x): the worker takes about 150 ms per set and the longest frame of those seconds is 16.68 ms, against one 146–155 ms frame per switch on the render thread. SSR on with MSAA 8x took 5,816 ms to compile on that card: a 6 s freeze before, nothing seen now.
  - Not kept, after measuring (2026-10-31): a wgpu pipeline cache (`Features::PIPELINE_CACHE`) kept on disk for these sets. On an RTX 5070 the driver's own disk cache already brings a set compiled before to about 160 ms; a filled wgpu cache gave the same times, and an empty one made the first run much slower (start 158 → 1,592 ms, next set 182 → 5,147 ms: the driver seems to skip its own cache when given one). The long compiles of the reports were first compiles, which no cache avoids. Worth trying again only with measurements on a driver without its own cache.
  - ⬜ later: compile the set's pipelines in parallel (rayon) to shorten the wait before the new samples show.
- 🟡 Water no longer turns white with some region environments (human report on the grid, 2026-10-31, task `water-blowout`; no issue): the water's final colour is capped like waterF.glsl (`min(vec4(1), max(color, 0))`, values that are not numbers cleaned); the region's water values are clamped to LLSettingsWater::validationList's ranges (fresnel 0–1, fog colour 0–1, normal scale 0–10, blur −0.5–0.5…); with enhanced water off the reflection follows waterF.glsl's wave_ibl (waves × normal scale) and the sun glint its unscaled, distance-flattened waves; with a normal scale of 0, wave_ibl is normalize(0), NaN in the Legacy Viewer, and Aurora takes the driver outcome the reported region shows (the probe lookup gives nothing: no reflection, only refraction and fog, a dark sea), enhanced water on or off; the probe reflection is blurred by the blur multiplier (doProbeSample); the water surface takes the Legacy air haze on every sky, enhanced water or not (hazeF.glsl over it after the water pass), through `ll_haze` like the terrain beside it, instead of Aurora's classic fog mix, whose colour was near white under the region's hazy, bright classic sky. Every sea changes a little: the distant water is darker and meets the sky on a sharper line, as in the Legacy Viewer. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_WATER_EEP` (with `AURORA_DEMO_SKY`). The region's water and sky values are logged on arrival (`water:` line, and the values clamped to the Legacy ranges). One sun on the water, as in the Legacy Viewer: the probes are read along the reflection ray as it is (doProbeSample), not flipped above the horizon; the glint is waterF.glsl's punctual light (pbrPunctual: `clamp(nl × spec, 0, 10)` × sunlit × shadow × atten, the blur multiplier as roughness, LLDrawPoolWater's specular colour as F0) instead of a highlight tinted before its clamp; the surface haze runs in hazeF.glsl's eye space (`ll_atmos_eye`), where its glow hotspot sits; and the sky dome is always drawn at LLSettingsSky's DOME_OFFSET 0.96 and DOME_RADIUS 15000 (getDomeOffset / getDomeRadius ignore the sky's values): a region sky with a 2000 m dome put Aurora's haze glow, and its reflection, well below the sun. The sky line of the log gives the sun texture and the dome sent. Validated by the human on the grid on 2026-11-01: the reported region's water, enhanced water off and on; then, with the review's changes, one sun on the water, its reflection on the glint.
  - ⬜ later: `ll_haze` multiplies by the whole `atten`, where hazeF.glsl blends by `atten.r` (its alpha): every hazed surface, in a separate PR.

- 🟡 Real night sky (human request, 2026-10-29; task `night-sky`; no issue; [PR #1560](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1560); validated by the human in demo and on the grid on 2026-10-30, on the version before the Milky Way speed-up, whose look is unchanged): the 8,920 stars of the HYG database v4.4 (CC BY-SA 4.0) down to magnitude 6.5, with their colours (B-V index), and a procedural Milky Way laid on the real galactic plane (bulge towards Sagittarius, Great Rift, star clouds), as seen from Paris (48.9° N, no light pollution). The sky turns around the Pole Star with the region's day cycle (the region sun's hour angle), the season follows today's date (the Sun's right ascension). Drawn in the sky shader, so the water and the reflection probes show it too; the catalogue is sorted into cube-map cells once at startup (`aurora-render/src/stars.rs`, frame binding 24), each star a Gaussian about a pixel wide whatever the field of view, slight scintillation, extinction towards the horizon; `world/night_sky.rs` gives the rotation. Brightness follows the sky's `star_brightness` with the Legacy curve (starsF.glsl: full from about 100). Preferences › Graphics › Environment › Night sky: Real sky (default) or Legacy. Deliberate differences from LLVOWLSky::initStars / LLDrawPoolWLSky::renderStarsDeferred (1,000 random stars on the upper dome, turning 0.01°/s about the vertical, added whatever the sky): the real sky, its Milky Way, and its stars drowned by a bright sky (they show at dusk, not at noon); the Legacy choice keeps a port of the Legacy stars (seeded, same colours, intensities and rotation). Before, Aurora drew hashed square dots on a 300-cell grid that were hard to see. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_NIGHT_SKY=real|legacy[:<azimuth>,<elevation>]`.
  - Maintainer review (2026-10-31): `stars.bin` rebuilt byte for byte from HYG v4.4 by the script; demo A/B against main. Fixed: stars seen through the water or in reflections (`sky_full`) take the middle pixel's size at right angles to their ray (they were drawn as dashes far from the view direction); the Legacy Viewer's stars keep their size in the sky (quads of 16 to 36 m on its 15 km dome, LLVOWLSky::updateStarGeometry), at least 0.75 px (their former size at the usual field of view), the stars in their former places; the device check asks for the five storage buffers the fragment stage now reads. ⬜ Left: a star brightness gain and a choice of latitude (presets and custom) in Preferences and Personal Lighting, in a follow-up PR; QA on the grid at night, under water and in photos.
  - 🟡 Sky place and star brightness (human request, 2026-10-31; task `night-sky-settings`; merged without a human test at the human's request): Preferences › Graphics › Environment › "Sky seen from" (Paris by default, London, New York, Los Angeles, Tokyo, Rio de Janeiro, Cape Town, Sydney, the Equator, the North Pole, Custom), "Latitude" (a preset's shown greyed, typed for Custom; moving it makes the place Custom) and "Star brightness" (0.5 to 4 times, 2 by default, the real stars only); the place and latitude also in Personal Lighting, so a photo's sky can be set from the photo window's light panel. Only the latitude counts: the hour follows the region's sun. Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_NIGHT_SKY_PLACE`. ⬜ Left: check on the grid at night, from a southern place, and in a photo through Personal Lighting.

- ✅ Texture animation set on a face the object does not have ([#1759](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1759); tester report, 2026-10-31; task `tex-anim-missing-face`; validated by the human on the grid on 2026-10-31, the object no longer flashes): a scripted mesh whose `llSetTextureAnim` targets face 2 of a one-face mesh (2×2 atlas at 20 frames/s) flashed in Aurora, the glow jumping between parts of the atlas, while the Legacy Viewer shows it still. Rule from LLVolumeGeometryManager::rebuildGeom (indra/newview/llvovolume.cpp): only faces in the TEXTURE_ANIM state use the animation matrix, set on every face for ALL_SIDES or on the animation's face alone; Aurora animated every face when the face was out of range. Now `tex_anim_targets` (scene/mod.rs) animates that face alone, so a missing face animates nothing; unit test of the three cases.

- ✅ "HDR and Emissive" switch ([#1355](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1355); task `hdr-emissive-switch`; validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-28): the Legacy Viewer's RenderDisableVintageMode, on by default, off in its Low and LowMid levels. Off: no automatic or manual exposure, no tone mapping, no sharpening (LLPipeline::gammaCorrect instead of tonemap), no emissive on opaque and alpha-masked PBR faces nor PBR terrain (HAS_EMISSIVE), reflection probes stored in 8 bits (RGB8). The tone mapping, mix, exposure and sharpening rows are greyed while it is off (Preferences › Graphics › Image and Light, the photo window's exposure). Potato and Low turn it off; settings version 28 moves a profile still exactly on either. Demo: `AURORA_HDR=0|1`, `AURORA_DEMO_PBR_EMISSIVE=1`. Deliberate difference: the Legacy Viewer also stops copying the scene for its screen-space reflections without HDR (copyScreenSpaceReflections is skipped, SSR reads a stale map); Aurora keeps SSR working. And where handleEnableHDR resets every reflection probe (the scene's reflections and ambient light went away, then came back probe by probe), Aurora draws them all again in place, each shown until its new capture replaces it; turned off, the exposure goes to 1 at once instead of easing (human feedback, 2026-10-28: the scene seemed to reload at each switch).
  - ⬜ later: grey the viewfinder's exposure dial too while the switch is off (it has no effect then).

Like LLViewerObject::getBakedTextureForMagicId, only a worn object that is neither a HUD nor an animated object takes its wearer's bake (`Scene::bake_wearer`); on the ground, on a HUD and on an animesh the placeholder is drawn as the texture asset it is. Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_BOM_REZZED=1` (a box of placeholders on the ground, with striped stand-ins for the grid's placeholder textures).

- 🟡 Crash in `egui_wgpu::Renderer::render` while driving in mouselook ([#1235](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1235), crash reports of 2026-10-28, 11 occurrences; task `egui-empty-frame-panic`). The labels (`label_depth`), the glass and the previews leave empty meshes under empty clips in the interface's primitives. When a frame has nothing else (mouselook hides the windows), egui-wgpu's `update_buffers` keeps the buffer slices of an earlier frame, and `render`, which takes one slice per mesh, panics as soon as that earlier frame had fewer meshes. Such a frame now hands `render` its paint callbacks only (`ui_frame::paint_jobs`); GPU test `a_frame_of_empty_meshes_renders_without_slices` reproduces the panic, then its fix. Validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-28 (mouselook with the crosshair off, labels around).
  - ⬜ to check on the grid by the reporter: long drives in mouselook with floating texts around, no crash

- 🟡 A masked face with a cutoff of 0 is drawn whole, like the Legacy Viewer (human report, 2026-10-26: a worn mesh dragon whose body faces have a Blinn-Phong Mask material with a cutoff of 0 on textures with an alpha channel; task `mask-cutoff-zero`; PR [#1149](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1149); validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-26: the dragon is drawn correctly). LL's materialF.glsl and pbropaqueF.glsl discard below `minimum_alpha` only (`alpha < cutoff`), so a cutoff of 0 keeps every texel; Aurora's shaders clamped the cutoff to 0.01 and cut out the texels of alpha 0. The clamp is gone from the depth prepass, the colour, reflection, glow, pick and impostor passes; alpha-to-coverage draws the whole face at a cutoff of 0. Covers glTF Mask materials with a cutoff of 0 too. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_MASK_ZERO=1`.

  - ⬜ later: the CPU face pick (HUDs, surface picks) still cuts the holes of a glTF Mask material with a cutoff of 0 (the legacy one is handled)

The Vulkan loader injects every implicit layer an installed program registers; the viewer now sets, at the start of `main` and before any thread, the variables Overwolf's two layers declare to disable them (`DISABLE_VULKAN_OW_OVERLAY_LAYER`, `DISABLE_VULKAN_OW_OBS_CAPTURE`; read by every loader version, unlike `VK_LOADER_LAYERS_DISABLE`), unless the user set them; OBS Studio's own capture layer is kept for streamers. `aurora-render/src/vulkan_layers.rs`, log line `Vulkan layers kept out of the viewer`, `AURORA_VULKAN_LAYERS=keep`. Not reproducible here (Overwolf not installed): only a tester with Overwolf can confirm. Proven here with `VK_LOADER_DEBUG=layer` and a throwaway probe that disabled OBS's layer the same way: the loader honours a variable the process sets itself (the layer no longer inserted), and `keep` brings it back.
  - ⬜ to check by QA / testers: on a PC with Overwolf running, the viewer starts and its log shows `Vulkan layers kept out of the viewer`; OBS Studio's game capture of Aurora still works; `AURORA_VULKAN_LAYERS=keep` loads Overwolf's layers back
- 🟡 Overlays kept out of the viewer (human request of 2026-10-25: in their testers' experience any overlay causes trouble; task `discord-overlay-white-screen`; PR authorised by the human on 2026-10-25). Implicit Vulkan layers, which the loader puts into every Vulkan program whether their program runs or not: Overwolf's (crash, #901) are still always disabled; the other overlays' layers are now disabled too unless Preferences › Graphics › Overlays › "Allow other programs' overlays" (off by default, applied at the next start; read from `settings.json` on `main`'s first lines, before any thread): the Steam overlay (`DISABLE_VK_LAYER_VALVE_steam_overlay_1`, manifest read on this PC), RivaTuner (`DISABLE_RTSS_LAYER`, which also crashes wgpu's device teardown elsewhere), the Epic Games overlay, Twitch Studio, FPS Monitor and PlayClaw. Kept: OBS Studio's game capture (and Wallpaper Engine's copy, same variable), ReShade, the drivers' layers (`VK_LAYER_NV_optimus`, `VK_LAYER_NV_present`, AMD's switchable graphics); `AURORA_VULKAN_LAYERS=keep` loads them all. Nothing unusual found on the viewer's side of the presentation (`Bgra8Unorm`, opaque, Mailbox or FIFO, frame latency 2): the common factor is these programs hooking the presentation. Legacy Viewer: no handling of overlays (OpenGL, where they inject DLLs). No visible change on a PC without these overlays (this one: only OBS's layers and the NVIDIA ones are loaded). Proven here with `VK_LOADER_DEBUG=layer` and the Steam overlay layer forced by its `ENABLE_` variable: kept out by default, loaded again with `AURORA_VULKAN_LAYERS=keep`, OBS's and the NVIDIA layers loaded in both runs.

The viewer now sets `VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE=*dzn*` at the start of `main` (the loader matches the manifest's file name, `dzn_icd.<arch>.json`, the compatibility pack's included: `loader_icd_scan`; loader 1.3.234 and later), unless the user set one of the loader's driver variables; when no Vulkan adapter is left without it, the renderer lets it back in and tries again. `aurora-render/src/vulkan_drivers.rs`, log line `Vulkan driver kept out of the viewer`, `AURORA_VULKAN_DRIVERS=keep`. Legacy Viewer: OpenGL, does not load Vulkan drivers. Not reproducible here (Dozen not installed): proven with `VK_LOADER_DEBUG=driver` and a throwaway build whose glob matched the NVIDIA manifest instead: the loader ignored `nv-vk64.json`, then the renderer let it back in and drew on the NVIDIA GPU.

- 🟡 White window with Discord's in-game overlay (reported to the human on 2026-10-24: the window stays white while the world's sound plays; task `discord-overlay-white-screen`). Discord registers no Vulkan layer: `DiscordHookHelper64.exe` injects `DiscordHook64.dll` into the running viewer when its overlay attaches or a Go Live stream captures the window, and the DLL patches `vkQueuePresentKHR`, DXGI and OpenGL in place (its own overlay drawing covers D3D9–12 and OpenGL only; its exclusions are a fixed list of executable names, so the viewer cannot refuse it). On this PC Discord's hook log shows it attached to Aurora during Go Live streams (`Hooked Vulkan`, no present handler created) with a normal image; the in-game overlay is not attached here (Aurora not a registered game), so the white window is not reproduced. First step, no visible change: `overlay_hooks.rs` lists the process's modules every 10 s and writes one warning per known hook that appears (Discord, Steam overlay, RivaTuner, OBS game capture), naming what to turn off, so a white or frozen window can be matched with the hook in the log, the crash report's warnings and the Dev Toolbox.

A driver that cannot be read is never called old. One log line (`graphics driver: … recent enough | out of date …`). The login screen (accounts and form alike) then shows a card edged in the caution colour in its top left corner: GPU, version found and minimum (or install date), "Get the <vendor> driver" (the vendor's official download page) and "Ignore for this driver" (`gpu_driver_dismissed`: a newer driver still too old warns again). The Legacy Viewer's OldGPUDriver notification (llappviewer.cpp) is a start modal whose test never fires (expected OpenGL version always zero). Demo `AURORA_DEMO_GPU_DRIVER=old|aged`.

  - 🟡 NVIDIA on Linux (task `linux-nvidia-driver-version`, no issue; PR [#1757](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1757)): the check never fired there, because the Linux driver's version has three numbers (`NVIDIA 570.86.16`) and only `major.minor` was read; and Linux has no installation date to fall back on. The third number is now left out, and Linux drivers are held to Linux minimums, as NVIDIA numbers its Linux branches on their own: 570.86 (570.86.16, the first Linux driver with the RTX 5090 / 5080, the same day as Windows' 572.16) and 470.256 for Kepler (470.256.02, that branch's last). Without them a Linux 570 driver, as recent as Windows' 572, would have been called old. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_GPU_DRIVER=old-linux`.

- 🟡 Mirrors show the scene and avatars (#654, 2026-10-21; task `mirror-hero-probe`; validated by the human in demo and on Agni on 2026-10-21: the mirror shows the place and the avatars): a tester's mirror showed a distorted view of the place and sky, without avatars, where the Legacy Viewer shows the reflection. Three causes, each against LLHeroProbeManager / tapHeroProbe (reflectionProbeF.glsl): (1) the mirror pass drew single-sided faces from both sides, so the mirror's own surface, a few centimetres in front of its plane, covered its whole image; the mirrored passes (mirror and water reflection) now keep the side facing their camera, as the Legacy Viewer's culled passes do (`fs_reflect`, `mirrored_pass`); (2) shiny legacy faces (shininess or legacy material environment) never took the mirror: they do now, the glossy environment by its glossiness and the legacy environment as fully glossy, like sampleReflectionProbesLegacy; (3) a mirror probe was also captured as an ordinary box probe, whose cube map (no avatars) showed wherever the mirror faded: it is a hero probe only now (LLVOVolume::updateReflectionProbePtr). The mirror weight follows tapHeroProbe: any surface inside the probe box (fading over its outer tenth), in front of the plane (from 5 cm behind), glossiness 0.75 to 1, whatever its normal (before: normal within ~30° of the plane's, roughness under 0.67); the planar image is looked up along the reflected ray through the mirror camera (`mirror_tap`), exact on the plane and like LL's cube map elsewhere. - 🟡 Normal maps keep their full strength on stretched UVs: the Legacy Viewer's tangent frame (2026-10-17; task `normal-map-tangents`; Refs #267). The human found the fine weave of their worn pants (five legacy materials, 2048 normal maps) much fainter than in the Legacy Viewer; ruled out with numbers: the textures' resolution (already full size), ambient occlusion (turned off: same look), the specular map (a uniform 19/255 grey, read correctly from the BC7 cache), the normal map alpha as glossiness and the lighting formulas (as materialF.glsl / softenLightF on a classic sky). The cause: `perturb_normal` (common.wgsl) derived the frame from screen-space derivatives (Schüler's cotangent frame) and scaled both axes by the longer gradient, which divided the relief along the axis where the texture coordinates are denser by the density ratio. It now builds per pixel the frame of LLVolumeFace::createTangents (read by materialF.glsl getNormal): T along dP/du, of unit length and orthogonal to the normal, B = cross(N, T) times the handedness, dP/du and dP/dv solved from the position and coordinate derivatives; no per-vertex data, no skinning cost, mirrored and skinned faces handled per pixel. `AURORA_TANGENTS=derivative` brings the former frame back, `alt` alternates them every second; `AURORA_DEMO_BUMP=tall|wide` stretches the demo's normal-mapped panel 4:1. Demo relief (high-pass RMS of the panel): `tall` 6.65 → 19.97, `wide` 21.88 → 21.58 (the restored axis is across the light there), square 14.56 → 14.57 (263 pixels of the image differ by more than 6).
  - Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-17 with `AURORA_TANGENTS=alt` on their pants, side by side with the Legacy Viewer ("en effet ça règle le souci").
  - ⬜ still to check on Agni: mesh bodies and other clothes, prims with stretched textures, mirrored UVs (the handedness), skinned faces in motion
  - 🟡 per-vertex tangents like the Legacy Viewer's (2026-10-17; task `mikktspace-tangents`): built with the geometry by the background tasks (`scene/tangents.rs`): Lengyel's for prims and sculpts (LLVolumeFace::createTangents), MikkTSpace for meshes (LLVolumeFace::cacheOptimize; `bevy_mikktspace` 1.0, MIT / Apache-2.0 with the reference's zlib notice, byte-identical to the C code), found in the mesh's upload proportions (`NormalizedScale`, now read, and written by our uploader as LLModel::writeModel does), vertices split where corners disagree (mirrored islands), Lengyel's past 16-bit indices. Packed in one byte, the `w` of the snorm normal (angle around the normal in 127 steps, 1.4° at most off; the handedness as the sign): the vertex stays 24 bytes. `object.wgsl` moves them like materialV / pbropaqueV (normal matrix, skinning matrix for rigged faces, tangent_space_transform for a PBR normal map's KHR rotation and scale signs) and `perturb_normal` uses them (B = sign × cross(N, T), as materialF getNormal), the per-pixel frame where a face has none (avatar bodies, terrain, animated PBR faces). `AURORA_TANGENTS=vertex` (default) `|pixel|derivative|alt` (vertex / pixel each second); `AURORA_DEMO_BUMP=sphere`: a low-poly ball with a normal map baked through its own tangents, round with `vertex`, faceted with `pixel`. Flat faces unchanged (panel: 0 pixels differ by more than 6). Measured: geometry of the demo crowd 22 MB used either way; over 2189 cached high-LOD meshes (8.0 M vertices) +3.65 % vertices from the splits, about +3 % of the geometry (about +4 MB for the 137 MB peak of the busiest region seen); MikkTSpace costs about 1.7 µs per vertex on the worker threads (6 ms per mesh on average, the weld 0.08 µs); GPU: objects pass 3.80 ms vertex vs 3.93 ms pixel at the demo crowd (59 M triangles, 5 alternated runs, within noise).
    - Tried by the human on Agni on 2026-10-17 with `AURORA_TANGENTS=alt`: no visible difference on their clothes (no regression); the gain shows on low-poly meshes with baked normal maps, as the demo ball shows.
    - ⬜ still to check on Agni with `AURORA_TANGENTS=alt`: low-poly objects with baked normal maps (no facets or seams), mirrored UVs, rigged faces in motion, PBR normal maps turned by a KHR rotation; the loading time at KB (MikkTSpace on the worker threads)
    - ⬜ later, if mesh loading shows it: MikkTSpace only for the meshes a normal-mapped face uses (the geometry is shared by objects of any material, so a face that gains a normal map would need its geometry rebuilt)

- 🟡 Textures loaded as finely as the Legacy Viewer loads them up close (2026-10-17; task `texture-camera-boost`; the human found normal maps flatter than in the Legacy Viewer). Investigation on the 57 normal maps of the human's grid caches: their relief (RMS angle between neighbouring texels) is 8.81° at full size, 7.66° one level down (−13 %), 6.10° two down (−31 %), and the grid logs show them decoded mostly at levels 1 to 3; Aurora sized every texture of a face by its object's diameter on screen, where the Legacy Viewer (LLViewerTextureList::updateImageDecodePriority, LLFace::calcPixelArea, LLFace::calcImportanceToCamera) measures the circle around the face from its nearest point and multiplies that area by up to TextureCameraBoost (8) for a face within 16 m and 10° of the view's centre (×4 at 16 to 32 m, ×2.9 nearby but aside, nothing beyond 96 m or while the camera moves faster than 10 m/s or turns faster than 1 rad/s): up to a level and a half finer. Ruled out with numbers: BC7 (−0.5 % relief, 0.38° mean error; detailed normal maps stay RGBA8), GTAO dropping `normal_map_occlusion` (same relief in demo, about one grey level lighter), the sampling (linear, green flipped as SL, renormalized) and the lighting (sun, ambient, specular and local lights use the mapped normal).
  - `scene/texture_importance.rs`: that size and those tables, the camera's mean speed over 50 frames (LLViewerCamera's velocity stats), applied to every map of a face (base, normal, specular / metallic-roughness, emissive); no boost under memory pressure (the Legacy Viewer divides it out with its discard bias). Repeats: the area is divided by the texture entry's smaller scale squared, within 0.0095 and 25 (TextureScale{Min,Max}AreaFactor), as the Legacy Viewer — before, the diameter was multiplied by the larger scale, so a repeated texture was loaded finer the more it repeated; glTF transforms are not counted, as there (a TODO in the Legacy Viewer). `AURORA_TEXTURE_SIZING=screen` brings the former sizing back.
  - Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=…,j2k=<cache\tex>,net=200`, the human's real textures through the local asset server, two runs each): 800 objects from the plaza, 10.1 / 10.4 → 11.7 / 11.7 MB downloaded, 3.8 / 4.3 → 8.2 / 8.2 Mpx decoded, `texture_mb` 11 / 12 → 20, `pages_mb` 70 / 71 → 82, no memory pressure; 200 objects with the first ones 5 m away, 4.0 → 5.2 MB, 4.7 → 10.3 Mpx, 34 → 41 textures at full size. Under a 96 MB budget (`AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=6000,6000`) the pressure steps behave as before (20 MB of textures and 168 MB of pages at step 7, 19 and 170 before).
  - KB (the human, 2026-10-17, this build, `AURORA_PROFILE=1`, two runs of about 2.5 min at the same place, 33-34 avatars, 11 drawn in full): with the boost `texture_mb` 7,941 / `pages_mb` 8,260 at 2 min 24 s, still climbing, pressure 0, 157 fps; with `AURORA_TEXTURE_SIZING=screen` 7,631 / 7,918 at 2 min 07 s, pressure 0, 157 fps: about +4 % of texture memory there (download counts not comparable: the second run had a warm cache, 937 vs 432 textures fetched). The human approved trying it.

The decode does not know a texture is used as a normal map: it would need the use passed to the streamer
- 🟡 Foliage, grass, fences and hair cut out of a texture no longer thin out with the distance (2026-10-17; task `alpha-coverage`; asked for by the human; validated by the human on Agni the same day). The mips of a texture were box-filtered (`build_mips`): a thin opaque shape averaged with the empty texels around it falls under the alpha cutoff a few levels down (demo foliage: 20% of the texels drawn at 256², 8.6% at 32², none from 16² on). A texture whose alpha is detected as a mask now keeps level 0's share of texels at or above the 0.5 cutoff at every level (`aurora_render::preserve_alpha_coverage`, Castaño, "Computing Alpha Mipmaps", 2010: the threshold of a level that keeps that share is read on its alpha histogram and the level scaled by cutoff / threshold; on a tie the fuller one): demo foliage 0.204, 0.275, 0.218, 0.177, 0.211, 0.250 down to 8². Done once at decode (about 1.4 ms for a 1024² mask on top of 2.2 ms of mips), stored in the transcoded cache (a mask's file says whether its coverage was kept: one made the other way is decoded again, once; the other textures' files stay valid); nothing at run time. The Legacy Viewer keeps the driver's box-filtered mips (LLImageGL), which thin out: a deliberate improvement. `AURORA_ALPHA_COVERAGE=0` keeps the plain mips; `AURORA_DEMO_FOLIAGE=1` (with `AURORA_DEMO_POS="80,100"`) shows the same panel at 5 to 60 m. Demo captures (SMAA and MSAA): the 10 and 20 m panels stay full, nothing else changes beyond the run-to-run noise.
