- 🟡 Ambient occlusion: GTAO as an option beside the Legacy method (human request of 2026-10-17, after the "To explore" line). Preferences › Graphics › Occlusion method: Legacy (default, the Legacy Viewer's screen-space occlusion, `ssao.wgsl`, its Low / High levels unchanged) or GTAO, with a GTAO quality Low / Medium / High / Ultra (`ao_method`, `gtao_quality`, default High). GTAO is a port of Intel's XeGTAO (MIT, notice in `shaders/gtao.wgsl` and NOTICE.md) in four compute steps from the single-sample depth prepass (`gtao.rs`): view depth in five levels (XeGTAO_DepthMIPFilter), the occlusion (slices of the hemisphere, horizon on both sides, cosine-weighted visible arc, falloff and thin occluder heuristic, normal from the depth with its edges), then XeGTAO's edge-aware 3 x 3 blur, which stands in for its temporal accumulation: the noise (Hilbert curve driving R2) is the same every frame, so nothing flickers. XeGTAO's constants (radius 0.73 m, falloff 0.615, final power 2.2…); slices and steps 2 / 2 / 3 / 9 and 2 / 2 / 3 / 3, Low at half resolution, two blur passes (one in Ultra). Its result goes where the Legacy one goes (`screen_ao`, same lighting, same "Show ambient occlusion" view); the normal map part the Legacy pass misses (`normal_map_occlusion`) is left out under GTAO. `AURORA_AO=legacy|gtao|alt[:<0-3>]` forces the method (and quality) for a launch, `alt` switching every second. `perf summary` gains `g_ssao` (the occlusion alone, inside `g_effects`; one of the per-effect timers point 6 of the audit of 2026-10-13 asks for). Demo (crowd of 40, 2560 × 1369, SMAA, 120 fps cap, the two methods alternated in the same session, medians): Legacy Low 0.08 to 0.15 ms, GTAO Low 0.10, Medium 0.24, High 0.31, Ultra 0.57 ms. In the occlusion view, Legacy is soft with wide halos, GTAO sharp in the folds of the avatars, under objects and in corners; on classic skies the lighting only lets the occlusion darken the ambient part (adjustIrradiance), so the image itself changes little there. Legacy mode: its code path is unchanged, and its capture of the plaza is within the demo's run-to-run noise (679 pixels over 8 levels from a capture of main; two captures of main differ by 438, two of this build by up to 19,982 where the torus turns). Validated by the human on 2026-10-17 ("on valide le gtao"). Still to check on the grid: fps at KB at each quality, a non classic sky, MSAA, the layout of the two Preferences rows.
  - 🟡 Specular occlusion from GTAO's bent normals (human request of 2026-10-17, task `gtao-specular-ssil`): the main pass also computes XeGTAO's bent normal (`XE_GTAO_COMPUTE_BENT_NORMALS`, the paper's algorithm 2, `XeGTAO_RotFromToMatrix`), blurred with the visibility (working targets in RGBA16F), and the result carries it in `.gba`. The shading (`specular_occlusion`, common.wgsl) turns it into the occlusion of the reflected ray: the visibility cone around the bent normal (cos = sqrt(1 - V)) against the specular cone of the roughness, the spherical caps' intersection (Jimenez et al. 2016; Oat and Sander 2007 with Filament's smooth overlap, NOTICE.md), faded out below a roughness of 0.3 as Filament does, so mirrors keep their reflection. Aurora's own two choices, after demo captures: measured against the open hemisphere around the same bent normal (counted raw, the rims of convex shapes lost their grazing reflections), and never darker than the visibility (raw, a polished metal went black and blotchy in an inside corner: what hides the sky is itself lit). Applied to the reflection of PBR faces (in place of the ambient occlusion on non classic skies, added on classic ones where the Legacy Viewer applies none) and to the glossy reflection of legacy materials; with GTAO only, the Legacy method's image is unchanged (`specular_occlusion` returns what the reflection took before). `AURORA_GTAO_SPECULAR=0|alt`. Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_PBR_METAL=1`, an inside corner of half-polished metal added left of the cube, `AURORA_DEMO_POS="131.5,131"`): the reflections fade into the corner's creases, about 7,000 pixels of 1,514,700 change, all in creases (corner, avatar sides, cube contact). Cost (crowd of 40, 2560 × 1369, 120 fps cap, PC shared with other viewers, three alternated runs each): `g_ssao` GTAO High 0.40 to 0.51 ms with the bent normal, 0.38 to 0.48 without, about +0.05 ms; the shading's part is within the noise (`g_objects` 0.50 / 0.52 ms in alternated seconds). After the human's first look (2026-10-17, "on rend ça propre"): the inside corner showed dark patches and soft waves on the metal with the effect on. Not the bent normal's precision (a 16-bit result changed nothing) nor its blur alone (three, then six more passes of the bent normal changed little): GTAO's own low-frequency patches in the visibility, which the specular occlusion shows on metal (no diffuse to hide them; the ambient occlusion only darkens the diffuse there), and the cone test's sharpness for a narrow lobe. Now the result carries a second visibility for the specular occlusion (`.g`, the bent normal's x and y in `.ba`), blurred with the bent normal three more times (`denoise_bent`, the occlusion's own `.r` untouched), and the lobe is never narrower than about 26° (cos 0.9): the corner darkens smoothly, without patches; the three passes bring GTAO High to about 0.6 ms (`g_ssao`, same crowd), 0.15 ms more (`.scratch/corner-fix.png` of the task: before above, after below, each with the effect on left and off right). Checked on the metal scene, its corner and the crowd, in SMAA and MSAA (separate runs on and off): the creases darken smoothly, by a few levels, nothing else changes. Seen by the human in demo on 2026-10-17 (first version), who asked for this cleanup and the intensity below. Still to check on the grid: fps at KB, avatar folds and skin, a non classic sky, MSAA.
  - 🟡 Screen-space indirect light with a visibility bitmask (human request of 2026-10-17, task `gtao-specular-ssil`; Therrien, Levesque and Gilet, "Screen Space Indirect Lighting with Visibility Bitmask", 2023, written from the paper). Preferences › Graphics › Indirect light (GTAO), off by default, with the GTAO method only (`screen_indirect_light`, Aurora's own). The main pass becomes `main_bitmask` (gtao.wgsl): on GTAO's slices and samples, 32 sectors per slice, uniform in the sine of the angle from the normal (so their count is the cosine-weighted visibility), each sample a surface 0.35 m thick that hides the sectors between its front and its back (thin objects no longer darken all that is behind them), within 1.5 m; a sample on the pixel's own plane hides nothing. Each sample lights the pixel, for the sectors it is the first to hide, with the previous frame's lit colour where it was (the scene copy, reprojected with the previous view-projection: `gtao::reprojection`), one bounce at physical strength; the light is blurred with the occlusion's edges, four passes more than it (grainy otherwise: two still left a grain on a lit box at the default strength), and added to the diffuse light of PBR, legacy and terrain surfaces, classic skies included (`screen_indirect`, common.wgsl; none in reflection passes). The visibility and its bent normal come from the sectors too (the mean angle of the open ones), so the specular occlusion above follows. `AURORA_SSIL=1|0|alt`; demo `AURORA_DEMO_BOUNCE=1` (a white floor and box between a red and a green wall): the box's sides and the foot of the walls take the light around them, subtle at strength 1 (a run at 8 times showed the walls and box coloured as expected). Cost (crowd of 40, 2560 × 1369, High, 120 fps cap, PC shared, three runs alternating every second): `g_ssao` 0.90 to 1.01 ms with it, 0.41 to 0.48 without, about +0.5 ms. With the cleanup below (more blur): 1.12 to 1.14 ms with it, 0.61 without. Its strength: Preferences › Graphics › Indirect light intensity, 0 to 4, default 1.5 (`screen_indirect_intensity`, reset with the section, greyed while the option is off; `AURORA_SSIL_INTENSITY=<0-8>` for a launch): captures at 1 (one physical bounce, hardly visible), 1.5, 2 (a glow starts around the foot of the box) and 4 (grainy, overdone). Seen by the human in demo on 2026-10-17 (first version, without the slider, which they asked for). Still to check on the grid: fps at KB, avatar folds and skin, a non classic sky, MSAA, a lit wall beside a floor in daylight. Not done: the samples' normals (light a surface sends away from the pixel still counts), a temporal accumulation (none in Aurora without TAA), light from beyond the screen or hidden by the front layer.
    - 🟡 the indirect light keeps GTAO's occlusion (human on 2026-10-17: "quand on l'active, j'ai l'impression que ça retire le GTAO, ça casse l'occlusion ambiante"; task `ssil-keeps-gtao`). `main_bitmask` replaced GTAO's main pass, so its visibility (thin samples hiding only what they cover) became the occlusion: softer in corners and contacts, and the bounce lit the creases back up. Measured in the AO view (`AURORA_DEMO_DEBUG=ao`, GTAO High, 1683 × 900) with the light off then on: the mean grey moved by 3.9 / 7.4 / 4.5 levels and 6.5 / 18 / 10.5 % of the pixels by more than 8 (crowd / `AURORA_DEMO_BOUNCE` / `AURORA_DEMO_PBR_METAL`). Now GTAO's `main` always runs and gives the occlusion, the edges and the bent normal; `main_bitmask` runs after it and writes only the light, which the shading weights by GTAO's occlusion (`screen_indirect`). The AO view is the same with the light on or off (no pixel off by more than 8, as between two runs of the same build), the bounce still lights the box and the walls' feet. Cost of the light (same view, 120 fps cap): `g_ssao` 0.53 → 0.62 to 0.66 ms (GTAO alone 0.23 to 0.31 either way). Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-17 ("c'est réglé").
    - 🟡 experimental (human decision of 2026-10-17): the warning triangle stays beside its label; off in every graphics level but Deluxe, which turns it on since settings version 21 (it was off in Deluxe in version 20); see the Deluxe line of the graphics presets
  - 🟡 the Deluxe graphics level takes GTAO at High quality (human decision of 2026-10-17): Aurora goes one step beyond the Legacy Viewer's Ultra list there; Potato / Low / Medium keep the occlusion off, High the Legacy method at Low, and the method outside the levels stays Legacy. The levels carry the method and the quality (`graphics_presets::Values`), which only count while the occlusion is on (and the quality only under GTAO), so a level still reads as itself whatever was chosen while it was off. Settings version 18: a profile still exactly on the former Deluxe (Legacy occlusion at its high level) moves to GTAO High once, any other keeps its occlusion (`upgrade_deluxe`). The photo quality boost keeps the method and adopts a change made while it is on. Validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-17.
    - 🟡 High took GTAO at Medium quality in settings version 20, then High quality in version 21, Medium Low quality and Deluxe Ultra quality (human decisions of 2026-10-17), see the Deluxe line of the graphics presets
  - 🟡 Temporal accumulation of GTAO (human request of 2026-10-19, task `gtao-temporal`): the fine grain left in the penumbra (folds of clothes, under objects) by the fixed noise, which the 3 x 3 blur alone could not take out; XeGTAO is made to run under TAA, and Aurora's default is SMAA. Now the noise moves every frame (XeGTAO's SpatioTemporalNoise, 288 per frame over 64 frames) and a `temporal` pass between `main` and the blur blends each pixel with its history (two RGBA16F targets holding the visibility, the specular visibility and the bent normal, and two R32Uint ones holding the view depth and the frame count): reprojected through its depth and the camera's motion (no motion vectors), bilinear over the four texels whose depth is the point's (slope-aware tolerance), else the same pixel when its depth there matches (our avatar, which the camera follows as it walks: without it the grain stayed on the walking avatar), clipped to the mean ± 1.25 standard deviations of the current 3 x 3 neighbourhood (no trail behind moving avatars), current frame weight 1 / (frames + 1), at least 0.1; NaNs are kept out of the history. The blur passes are unchanged and contacts stay sharp. A frame without history (first frame, resize, quality change, photo frame or tile, a frame after one without GTAO or without the previous camera) samples four times more slices, so a photo looks like the live view (it showed the old grain otherwise). The indirect light keeps its fixed noise (not accumulated). `AURORA_GTAO_TEMPORAL=0|1|alt` (0: the noise fixed again, as before). Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_DEBUG=ao`, High and Ultra): grain gone with a still camera, an orbiting one (`AURORA_DEMO_CAMERA=drift`), our avatar walking (`AURORA_DEMO_DOUBLECLICK=walk`) and walking before a fixed camera (no ring lagging behind the feet); photos at 1600 x 900 and in 8 tiles. Cost (RTX 4090 shared, 1600 x 900, SMAA, crowd of 40, 120 fps cap, `alt` in one run): `g_ssao` High 0.23 → 0.26 ms, Ultra 0.37 → 0.39 ms; memory 16 bytes per occlusion pixel more (about 23 MB at 1600 x 900, 56 MB at 2560 x 1369). Seen by the human on the grid on 2026-10-19 ("mieux": GTAO High, SMAA, one teleport in the session, `g_ssao` median 0.76 ms at 1278 x 1360). Still to check on the grid: moving avatars and objects before a still camera, fast camera turns, a non classic sky, a photo.
    - 🟡 horizontal stripes and blocks in the occlusion on Linux with the NVIDIA driver (615), crawling with the accumulation (task `gtao-hilbert-nvidia-linux`, 2026-10-30; validated by the human on the grid on 2026-10-30, GTAO on Deluxe on an RTX 5090: the blocks are gone). The noise's Hilbert index (`hilbert_index`, gtao.wgsl) came out wrong for whole quadrants of the 64 x 64 tile there, so the noise formed rows; the nested `if` that mirrors and swaps the coordinates (XeGTAO's `HilbertIndex`) is now written with `select` over the six bits, the same steps, which give the index the CPU test computes (`hilbert_index_walks_the_tile`). Other drivers compute the same index as before.
  - 🟡 a photo drawn in tiles showed a thin dark line along the tiles' borders with GTAO (task `tiled-photo-ao-seam`, validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-19; there before the accumulation, with `AURORA_GTAO_TEMPORAL=0` too). Each tile was drawn alone with its off-centre projection, so the screen-space passes read no depth beyond it: GTAO took the border row it read again past the edge for a wall (the horizon search, the normal and the edges from depth), and the contact shadows lost the casters across the border. Now each tile is drawn with a guard band of 128 photo pixels on the sides it shares with another tile (`snapshot::TILE_GUARD`, at most an eighth of the side a pass can draw, the drawn origin on an even pixel for GTAO at half resolution), then cropped; the photo's own edges and photos in one pass are unchanged, and the tiles are planned so that they fit the card with their bands. Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_SNAPSHOT=save:3200x1800:png`, `AURORA_DEMO_SNAPSHOT_TILE=1024`, `AURORA_AO=gtao:2`, `AURORA_DEMO_DEBUG=ao`, `AURORA_GTAO_TEMPORAL=0`), tiled photo against the same photo in one pass: mean difference in the first pixel along the borders 21.9 → 0.10 levels of 255 (0.43 over the whole photo, the demo's animations), the line gone; in the sun shadow view with the contact shadows on (`AURORA_DEBUG_SHADOWS=1`, `AURORA_CONTACT_SHADOWS=1`), 0.62 → 0.06 along the borders (0.16 elsewhere). Photos in one pass identical, old and new builds alternated (0.002 levels, as between two runs of the same build). Unit tests of the plan (bands on the shared sides only, every pass within the limits down to the smallest ones) and of the stitch; `check.ps1` green (3,902 passed, 26 ignored). To verify on Agni with the photo window's tiled photos (see Photo window, part 1: "no tile seam").
  - 🟡 Motion vectors for GTAO's history (2026-10-30, PR [#1702](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1702)): the history was reprojected through the camera only, so moving avatars and objects dragged their old occlusion or lost their history. The renderer keeps last frame's model matrices and joint palettes on the GPU (`motion_history.rs`: one compute gather of the records' matrices and one palette copy per frame, only while GTAO reads the mesh normals, no readback; the first frame that reads them again starts the history again; slots reused by a new object or skeleton start from their current pose, and a region change or origin shift cuts the history). While GTAO uses the mesh normals, the depth prepass writes each pixel's screen motion (unjittered, in uv) beside the normal; GTAO's `temporal` pass reprojects with it, keeps the exact depth test for what only the camera moved and accepts the span between the old and new depth for what moved on its own. With the motion the history holds about thirty frames (current weight at least 0.03; 0.1 as before with `AURORA_GTAO_NORMALS=depth`, which writes no motion), at half resolution the pixel takes the motion of the one of its four full-resolution texels that moved least apart from the camera, and the current frame weighs at least 0.1 where the point moves on screen, so the grain is quieter without trails. Where the point moved on its own its occlusion can change because it moved (a hem lifting off the ground), so there the history is shorter (current weight at least 0.2) and clipped tighter (0.6 standard deviations instead of 1.25). `AURORA_DEBUG_MOTION=1` shows the motion vectors. Cost (RTX 5090, 3840 x 2160, Deluxe, GTAO Ultra, crowd of 100, medians of two runs each): `gpu` 2.815 → 2.810 ms, `g_depth` 0.100 → 0.112 ms, `g_ssao` 1.284 → 1.311 ms (run-to-run noise ±0.04). Tried on the grid by the PR's author on 2026-10-30 (GTAO on Deluxe, with the Hilbert index fix of its own PR); to validate by the team. TAA does not use the motion yet.
    - ⬜ later: TAA reprojects with the motion vectors (separate PR).
  - 🟡 GTAO from the mesh's smooth normals ([#993](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/993), 2026-10-26; task `gtao-mesh-normals`; validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-26): the normal GTAO rebuilt from the depth was the flat triangle's, so low-poly meshes showed their facets in the occlusion. When GTAO is shown, the depth prepass also draws the vertices' smooth normal (`vs_depth_normal`, `gtao::NORMAL_FORMAT`), and GTAO and its indirect light read it (`surface_normals`, gtao.wgsl); on each slice the horizons drop by the angle between the triangle and the smooth tangent plane (`facet_lift`, at most 45°), else a facet occluded itself under the smooth normal (a ring along round silhouettes). `AURORA_GTAO_NORMALS=depth|alt` to compare; the Legacy method is unchanged. Prepass +0.005 ms at 1600 x 900 in demo. Faint facet edges can remain where the lift changes from one triangle to the next.
    - ⬜ to check on Agni (QA testers): GTAO on, under a sky with strong ambient light, low-poly smooth meshes (round prims, avatar bodies, furniture): no square facets in the occlusion, no dark ring along their silhouettes; contact occlusion under objects and in corners as before.
    - 🟡 facets still visible on 0.8.2 under a sky with strong ambient light and no probe ambiance (reported on [#993](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/993) on 2026-10-29; task `gtao-facet-edges`, PR [#1556](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1556); validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-29, the old and new corrections side by side, grid test skipped): the facet correction measured occluders from the flat triangle's plane, which changes from one triangle to the next, so real occlusion jumped at the triangles' edges (patches on the avatar's back and skirt), and concave creases drew the mesh's edges as lines (the coarse depth levels were checked: not the cause). Now each sample occludes only as much as it stands above the triangle's own plane (`above_facet` in gtao.wgsl: nothing on it, fully from 30° above it, smoothly between), its height still measured from the smooth plane; the indirect light's bitmask the same; XeGTAO's clamp of the horizon angles around the normal, which only the old correction applied, now applies always. Demo, GTAO, `AURORA_DEMO_SKY=1,0.8,1.2`, indirect light off: the patches and crease lines are gone and the occlusion keeps its strength (lit avatar 160.8, before 161.1, Legacy 161.6). With the indirect light on (intensity 4) GTAO looks much lighter than Legacy, with or without this change
    - ✅ facets still visible on 0.8.4 in concave folds (a pony body's chest between the front legs, under the chin; reported on [#993](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/993) on 2026-10-31; task `gtao-concave-facets`, PR [#1712](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1712)): #1556 still weighed each sample by its height above the flat triangle's plane, which jumps at every edge, and a real occluder in that 0–30° band counted more on one triangle than on the next. The weight is now measured from the smooth normal (`above_surface` in gtao.wgsl: nothing within 20° of the smooth tangent plane, fully from 44°), in the occlusion and the indirect light's bitmask; the flat normal is no longer rebuilt when the mesh normals are on. Bands of 10° (crease lines on the demo's large low-poly shape), 15° (one line left), 20° and 25° (shallow folds lighter) compared in demo on the avatar and on the reporter's pony mesh (`AURORA_DEMO_IMPORT_FILE`); 20° kept. Occlusion view, the pony's chest: mean grey 211.9 before, 216.1 after, Legacy 211.8. Validated by the human on the grid on 2026-10-31.
  - ⬜ later: the occlusion of the reflection passes (none today, Legacy included)
- ✅ Contact shadows of the sun (human request of 2026-10-17): Preferences › Graphics › Contact shadows, beside Projector shadows, off by default and only with the sun shadows (`contact_shadows`, an Aurora option beyond the Legacy Viewer). A port of Bend Studio's screen space shadows (Days Gone; Apache-2.0, notice in `shaders/contact_shadows.wgsl` and NOTICE.md): from the single-sample depth prepass, each workgroup is a wavefront of 64 pixels along a ray towards the light's point on screen, in up to eight dispatches laid out around it (`build_dispatch_list`, Bend's `BuildDispatchList`); a pixel is in shadow when one of the 60 depths before it along the ray, made perspective-correct towards the light, lies within 0.5 % of its depth (Bend's defaults: bilinear threshold 2 %, contrast 4, 4 hard and 8 fading samples). Integer texel loads in place of a clamp-to-border sampler, a whole wavefront of sky leaves early, the target is emptied first (the pixel under the light's point stays lit). The shading takes the darker of the shadow map and the mask (`sun_shadow` in common.wgsl) for the opaque faces and the terrain of the main view; water, reflections, probes and impostor pictures keep the shadow map alone; the shadow view (`AURORA_DEBUG_SHADOWS`) shows them. `AURORA_CONTACT_SHADOWS=0|1|alt` for a comparison; `perf summary` gains `g_contact` (inside `g_effects`). Demo (crowd of 40, 2560 × 1369, SMAA, 120 fps cap, alternated in the session, RTX 4090 shared with other runs): 0.19 to 0.26 ms; thin shadows where arms meet the body, under the waist on the skirts, at the base of the lamp posts and on the crowd's hands, 0.4 to 0.8 % of the pixels changed in the frame, the same under MSAA. Off, the shading reads nothing new (the mask term is 1) and no pass runs. Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-17 ("ça rend la scène plus crédible pour les ombres").
  - ✅ Feet that cast nothing (human on Agni on 2026-10-17: "sur les pieds, sur certains avatars ça fonctionne, pas sur d'autres"). The pass read the depth prepass, which holds only the opaque and masked faces: blended faces (the many mesh bodies, shoes and hair whose faces are blended though they look opaque) and the impostor cards (avatars past the full ones) were not in it, so they neither cast nor received. Now, when the contact shadows draw, the prepass is copied and the blended faces opaque enough (texture alpha × color alpha ≥ 0.5, `fs_depth_contact`, both sides) and the impostor cards (`fs_impostor_depth`) are drawn into the copy, which the pass reads; a blended face that opaque receives them too (`frame.contact.y`). Demo `AURORA_DEMO_FEET=opaque|blend` (shoes on every foot and two blocks on the ground, one blended): with `AURORA_CONTACT_SHADOWS=prepass` (the former casters) the blended block is missing from the depth the pass reads, now it is there (a capture of that depth in contours) and takes the contact shadows as the opaque block does. Cost with the copy and the extra casters: 0.17 to 0.18 ms in the same crowd. Validated on Agni on 2026-10-17: the feet that had none now have them.
  - ⬜ later: some avatars' feet still get no contact shadow on Agni after the fix above (human, 2026-10-17: "il en manque encore quelques uns"). To investigate: identify those feet and shoes (Preferences › Nearby objects › Describe next to them: alpha mode, rigged or not, worn hover or sinking into the ground, impostor or drawn in full), then check them against the known limits: thick casters only near their edges, hovering feet, blended faces under 0.5 of alpha, faces the copied depth skips
  - 🟡 hoof- or shoe-shaped outlines instead of a shadow under thick casters, worst at a low sun ([#988](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/988), 2026-10-26; task `contact-shadow-artifacts`; validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-26, the grid check left: with the contact shadows on and a low sun ahead of the camera, hooves and shoes standing or hovering slightly over the ground get a shadow under them, not a ring of their outline, and the shadows' borders show no pixel steps, from a low camera and from above). Cause: each depth counted as a shell of 0.5 % of its distance (Bend's surface thickness, 1.5 cm at 3 m), so a ray that went under a hoof or a shoe, through its body behind the visible faces, was stopped only where it grazed their edges, and the ground took the caster's outline instead of its shadow; seen with the sun ahead of the camera (the ray recedes). Now an occluder is taken as deep as the ray went under it: a surface lying between the pixel's own depth and the ray's shadows, up to 5 cm behind it (`OCCLUDER_DEPTH`, `depth_delta` in contact_shadows.wgsl; one shell again from 10 m on, and when the ray comes towards the camera). A fixed depth was tried first and dropped: each caster darkened the ground behind it with a copy of its silhouette, so a surface nearer than the pixel keeps the shell; with one layer of depth a ray passing beside a caster still looks like one going under it, which a 15 cm cap showed as a ledge of shadow beside the hoof, 5 cm keeps within the shadow's edge. `AURORA_CONTACT_SHADOWS=shell` gives the former window; demo `AURORA_DEMO_SUN=<azimuth>,<elevation>` turns the sun (the times of day never put it ahead of the demo camera) and `AURORA_DEMO_FEET` gains a hoof on the ground and a shoe hovering 2 cm. Demo (shadow view, `AURORA_DEMO_SUN=0,12`, close-up on the shoe): with `shell` the ground under the shoe stays lit with a thin dark line along the sole, the issue's look; now it takes the shoe's contact shadow; with the sun behind the camera (times of day 2 and 3, crowd of 40) the image does not change beyond run-to-run noise. Cost (crowd of 40, sun ahead, 120 fps cap, 4 alternated passes, shared GPU): `g_contact` median 0.194 → 0.210 ms. Seen from above, the gap under the hovering shoe stayed a dotted line one pixel wide (human, 2026-10-26: "un trait"), right in itself (that gap is in shadow) but hard, like the steps on curved bodies: the mask is now softened before the shading reads it, a 5 × 5 tent over the pixels of the same surface (a neighbour counts as far as its depth lies on the pixel's plane, 1 % of its depth), so no shadow spreads from the ground onto a caster nor the reverse (`contact_shadows_filter.wgsl`, the tile read once into workgroup memory; `AURORA_CONTACT_SOFT=0` for the hard mask). Demo: the dotted line and the steps on our avatar's sides are gone, no halo around the avatars of the crowd; cost about +0.07 ms (`g_contact` median 0.234 → 0.301 ms, 5 alternated passes, same crowd, shared GPU). Feet floating more than the window above the ground keep the gap
  - ✅ graphics presets: High and Deluxe turn them on (High since settings version 21; human decisions of 2026-10-17, see the Deluxe line of the graphics presets)

  - 🟡 contact shadows shorter in a saved photo than in the viewfinder ([#1662](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1662), 2026-10-31; task `photo-contact-shadows`; validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-31, 8K photos against the viewfinder; QA's check of the reporter's scene left). Cause: Bend's 60 samples are a length in pixels, so a 4K or 8K photo, 3 to 7 times the viewfinder's height, had shadows 3 to 7 times shorter in the image (and half again with Photo quality's supersampling). A photo now marches 60 times its height over the viewfinder's (`snapshot::viewfinder_scale`, the window's height or width over the photo's aspect, times the render scale; `FrameParams::photo_scale`), its 4 hard and 8 fading samples in proportion, up to 480, in a pipeline of its own made on its first frame (`shader_source`: Bend's four constants rewritten; kept for the next photo of the same scale); the window keeps Bend's shader untouched (a count read at run time, tried first, made the window's pass 0.45 → 0.84 ms). A photo drawn in tiles widens its guard band to the rays (`contact_tile_reach`). Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_FEET=opaque`, `AURORA_DEMO_SUN=0,12`, `AURORA_DEBUG_SHADOWS=1`, `AURORA_DEMO_POS=129,134`, window 1600 x 900 at 150 %, `AURORA_DEMO_SNAPSHOT=save:7680x4320`, 192 samples): the streaks behind the hoof and the shoe in the 8K photo now have the window's length, in one pass and in 15 tiles (`AURORA_DEMO_SNAPSHOT_TILE=2048`); 8K photo 370 → 440 ms in one pass, 540 → 600 ms in tiles. Window unchanged: `g_contact` 0.454 → 0.444 / 0.454 ms (crowd of 40, 2400 x 1350, 120 fps cap)

Probable cause: GTAO's radius (0.73 m) has no limit in pixels, so near the camera its horizon search reaches hundreds of pixels past the 128-pixel guard band (sized for "beyond 9 m"); not reproduced in demo yet (the far views show no step)
- 🟡 Specular anti-aliasing (human request of 2026-10-17, task `specular-aa`): Preferences › Graphics › Specular anti-aliasing, under Anti-aliasing, on by default (an Aurora improvement beyond the Legacy Viewer; `specular_aa`). Geometric specular anti-aliasing (Kaplanyan & Hoffman 2016, in Filament's form: `specular_aa_roughness` in common.wgsl, variance 0.15, kernel capped at alpha² 0.2) widens a highlight where the shading normal turns faster than a pixel: the GGX lobe of a PBR face, and for a legacy material its glossiness through the GGX alpha of the same lobe width and back (`specular_aa_gloss`: unchanged without variance). Only what a pixel cannot resolve counts: below a variance of 0.001 (a normal turning about 0.06 rad per pixel) nothing changes, so a polished ball up close keeps its pinpoint highlights (without that floor, the demo's polished sphere, 110 pixels across, had its highlights eight times larger). The variance a normal map's coarser mips lose (Toksvig, from the length of the sampled normal before it is renormalized) joins it, from 1.5 % short. `AURORA_SPECULAR_AA=0|1|alt`; `AURORA_DEMO_SHIMMER=1` adds a long glossy plate with a fine repeated normal map. Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_PBR_METAL=1`, slow orbit, 13 frames 25 apart, 1683 × 900, SMAA): about 450 pixels change, on the rims of the polished spheres, where the frame-to-frame flicker goes down a little (temporal deviation 11.5 → 11.2 there); flat and gently curved surfaces are the same image; `gpu` and `g_objects` the same within noise (crowd of 40, two alternated passes each). The demo has little that shimmers: the real test is on the grid. Validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-17 (on by default confirmed).
  - ⬜ to check on Agni, on and off: fine normal maps on glossy cloth, metal and hair seen from a few metres to far, the rims of jewellery and small shiny objects while the camera turns; that nothing large and smooth loses its sharp highlights; the Legacy look of a glossy legacy material up close
  - ⬜ later: the water's highlights (water.wgsl keeps its own specular) and the legacy shiny of faces without a material (TE shiny) do not take it yet
- 🟡 Bloom, Aurora's own (human request of 2026-10-17; the Legacy Viewer has only the glow of faces with a glow value, which stays as it is): Preferences › Graphics › Bloom (off by default) and Bloom strength (0.05 to 1, 0.5), beside Glow (`bloom`, `bloom_strength`). The mip chain of Jimenez, "Next Generation Post Processing in Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare" (SIGGRAPH 2014) (`bloom.rs`, `shaders/bloom.wgsl`): the light over a threshold extracted at half resolution with the 13-tap downsample and a Karis average against fireflies (`fs_bloom_prefilter` in `post.wgsl`), smaller levels down to a short side of 8 pixels (six at 2560 × 1369), then each one blurred by a 3 x 3 tent and added to the level above it. The post pass takes the share `strength` of the light over the threshold away from each pixel and puts it back spread by the levels, five times brighter: Second Life light seldom goes far past white (classic skies are not tone mapped), so a halo of that light alone hardly shows (demo: gains 1 and 3 barely visible, 6 a clear halo). Threshold 0.8 in exposed units with a soft knee of 0.3, on every tone mapper; after the glow, before FXAA / CAS / SMAA, so neither the interface nor the HUDs bloom; none under a debug view. Its levels exist only while it is on. `AURORA_BLOOM=0|1|alt`; `perf summary` gains `g_bloom` (inside `g_post`). Demo, 2560 × 1369, 120 fps cap, on and off alternated in the session: 0.07 ms on the plaza, 0.09 ms in a crowd of 40 (`g_post` 0.21 → 0.32 ms). Off, the post pass reads the scene exactly as before. Validated by the human in the demo and on Agni on 2026-10-17 ("top le bloom !!").
  - 🟡 experimental (human decision of 2026-10-17): off in every graphics level, Deluxe included, and by default; the warning triangle beside its label. It turned on with Deluxe for a few hours (settings version 19), the version 20 migration turns it off again for a profile still exactly on that Deluxe
  - ⬜ later, not now (human on Agni on 2026-10-17): in a busy region the image is burnt, far too bright, with the bloom on, and already very bright without it. Compare the exposure and the sky brightness there with the Legacy Viewer side by side (classic or non classic sky, probe ambiance, legacy gamma, exposure, glow), then the bloom threshold against Second Life's values brighter than white
  - ⬜ still to check on the grid: MSAA, a non classic sky (tone mapped), a photo in several tiles (each tile blooms on its own, as the glow)
## Optimisation

Frames per second, hitches, video memory and loading times. One PR per item, with the before / after measurement (`AURORA_PROFILE=1`, see [docs/TESTING.md](docs/TESTING.md#profiling)). The performance lines that were in "Rendering" (culling audit) and in "Interface" ("Perf, from this measurement run") were gathered here on 2026-10-12, without any change to their text.

- 🟡 **GPU cost of busy regions at 4K** (#1489; task `gpu-cost-4k`). On the grid at 3840 × 2054 (RTX 5070, busy region) the frame took 22–27 ms of GPU: objects 8.7, transparent 3.3–7.2, effects 6.5 (GTAO 4.8–5.0), shadows 2.5. Demo, deluxe preset, 2880 × 1620 against 5760 × 3081: GTAO ultra grows with the pixels (5.2 → 19.5 ms), objects ×2.7, contact ×3.6, post ×2.7; shadows hardly move.
  - 🟡 GTAO at half resolution from 2560 × 1440 (PR #1778), every level (`gtao::quality_for`), with a depth-aware upsample (`upsample`, `upsample_il` in gtao.wgsl: the four nearest texels weighted bilinearly and by their depth against the pixel's), which low quality now takes too instead of the bilinear stretch. 3840 × 2054, deluxe, crowd of 200: GTAO 8.92 → 2.54 ms, 55.7 → 87.7 fps; captures the same at 1:1 and 2× zoom (mean difference 1.34/255 in the avatar, against 1.68 for the bilinear stretch). The Legacy Viewer's occlusion is a few taps in the sun light pass at full resolution (sunLightSSAOF.glsl, aoUtil.glsl). Human validation on the grid, 2026-10-31 (same busy region and spot, 3840 × 2054, GTAO ultra, dev build): GTAO 4.8–5.0 → 1.63 ms, effects 6.5 → 3.3 ms, the frame without the transparent faces (they follow the view) 19.35 → 16.25 ms, 37–42 → 46 fps; no outline around avatars or objects; the window resized down to 1200 × 840 and back across the threshold without a visible change. ⬜ QA: an AMD and an Intel card at 4K, and a 1440p screen (on the threshold).
  - ⬜ objects and transparent faces at 4K: what their shading costs per pixel, and the overdraw of layered alpha (the demo has too little of it)
  - ⬜ The sun shadow at 4K (measured 2026-11-01, task `gpu-shading-4k`, no PR): about 2.7 ms of the objects pass (6.3 ms) and 1.5 ms of the transparent faces at 3840 × 2054 (deluxe, `AURORA_DEMO_TEXTURES=9000`, `AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=200`); local lights, atmospherics and caustics 0.4–1.1 ms each. Dead ends: fewer samples (16 cost as much as 49; the same filter in 16 weighted samples is slower); a shader without the PBR-sky branch (no gain); the shadow once per pixel in a compute pass over the prepass depth (objects −1.8 ms, the pass +1.6 ms); skipping its filter by an 8 × 8 min/max of the shadow map (too few pixels qualify).
  - ⬜ The four passes of rigged transparent faces (`RiggedBlendDepth::Layers`, #1300): 1.9 of 3.8 ms with `AURORA_DEMO_HAIR=8` and the crowd at 4K, 0.23 ms at 1080p (pixels, not vertices). Fewer passes without bringing back #935, #948, #1300 or #556: a task of its own, with QA checks on real hair.

- 🟡 **Frame pacing: the input no longer waits in the frame queue** (#1484, PR #1646). When the GPU set the pace, the main thread read the input, then waited for the render thread, which waited for the swapchain: windows dragged behind the cursor and the camera lagged at 60 fps, but not with the frame limiter (which leaves the stages empty). `aurora-render/src/pacing.rs`: once frame N is handed over, the main thread waits for the news that the GPU has finished frame N−1 (at the limiter's place, before the next input, at most 100 ms), so at most one frame waits for the GPU. The news comes from the render thread (a poll at the start of each job, else a device wait after it presents): a device wait on the main thread stalled the render thread's `present` (measured: 22 ms a frame). Demo, GPU-bound (`AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=200`, `AURORA_GRAPHICS_PRESET=deluxe`, 3840 × 2160, no cap, dev build): input to presentation 93 ms → 27 ms, p95 frame 140 → 74 ms, 21 → 20–22 fps (shared PC, within noise); at a 60 fps cap nothing changes (`pace` 0.5 ms). Simulated GPU-bound 60 fps: input to GPU done 61 → 32 ms, same frame time. (A feedback sleep on the measured waits was tried first: it oscillated in the simulation.) `wait_render` now counts the real back-pressure wait (it is taken before the packet is built); `pace` and `input` (input to presentation) added to the `perf summary`; `AURORA_FRAME_PACING=0` to compare. The Legacy Viewer has a single thread between input and swap (`LLAppViewer::mainLoop`). Maintainer A/B in demo on 2026-10-30 (crowd of 200, deluxe, 5760 x 3240, GPU-bound, 3 runs each): 46 fps both ways, input to present 44 ms without pacing, 6 to 9 ms with it. ⬜ Grid check by the QA team: in a busy region with no frame limit, a floater dragged in circles and the camera orbit follow the mouse; the frame rate stays the same as with `AURORA_FRAME_PACING=0`.
  - 🟡 **The wait only when the GPU alone sets the pace** (#1711, since deleted on GitHub; PR #1774). The paced period is `max(M, (M + R + G) / 2)` against `max(M, R, G)` (M main thread, R render thread, G GPU): free when `G ≥ M + R`, up to a third slower when the three stages are close (simulated: 125 → 95 fps at 8 / 6 / 7 ms, 83 → 63 fps at 12 / 9 / 11 ms), that is a busy region on a fast card or two viewers on one card, the 0.8.4 frame rate drops. `pacing::Gate` keeps both waits (main thread and render thread) on only while the smoothed GPU time covers the other two, with 5 % margins; off without GPU timestamps. `AURORA_FRAME_PACING=always` keeps the 0.8.4 wait on every frame, to compare. Also fixed: the main thread's back-pressure wait was overwritten by the hand-over's (`wait_render` read 0, `packet` counted the wait as work), which kept the gate off. Demo, dev build, RTX 5070, `AURORA_DEMO_CROWD`, no cap, immediate present: CPU-heavy (`AURORA_CPU_CULL=1`, 400 avatars, 1100 × 620) gate 180.6 fps, always 155.0, off 181.2; GPU-bound (200 avatars, default window) gate 101.0 fps and input to present 11.8 ms, always 101.9 / 11.7 ms, off 100.9 / 27.8 ms; two viewers at once (GPU-bound) 112 fps together with the gate or always, 105 off. Human validation on the grid, 2026-10-31 (busy region, RTX 5070, 3840 × 2054, no vsync, dev build): GPU-bound there (22–27 ms of GPU a frame), the gate kept the wait on and the frame rate followed the GPU time as with `always` (36.9 fps at 26.5 ms, 41.6 fps at 22.7 ms, different views). ⬜ Grid check by the QA team where the CPU stages are close to the GPU (smaller window, lower preset, or two viewers on one card): gate against `AURORA_FRAME_PACING=always` and `0`.

The follow-up (BC7 in video memory, disk cache of already transcoded textures, faster JPEG2000 decoding) is in progress in the line "Textures: gain loading time and performance by moving away from JPEG2000 on the viewer side" of "Rendering", left in its place as long as its task is open; to be brought back here afterwards.
    - 🟡 texture budget lowers only what is over its goal ([#1557](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1557), task `tp-arrival-fps`, 2026-10-30; PR #1802): the human's grid logs of a busy region showed the pressure going 0 -> 1 for 13 MB over a 4.2 GB target, every texture finer than its size on screen lowered (pages 4.2 GB -> 1.5 GB), the step back at 0 five seconds later and the textures loaded again as the camera moved, every few minutes and up to every 10 s. A step now lowers the largest textures first and only until the pages are back under 85 % of the target (`texture_budget::lowering_goal`, under the 90 % a step down waits for). Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=3000`, `AURORA_TEXTURE_BUDGET_MB=3000`): 461 textures lowered and 2.5 GB kept instead of 3,571 lowered and 105 MB kept, same frame rate; a scene that does not fit (512, 96) still climbs the steps to the same end. Does not explain #1557's 1–2 FPS on its own: data from the reporter is still needed.
    - 🟡 the budget given out is the driver's lowest of the last minute (#1557, #1713, task `tp-arrival-fps`, 2026-11-01; PR #1802; `vram::BudgetFloor`, `BUDGET_WINDOW`): a drop counts at once, a rise once it has held 60 s. Grid runs of 2026-10-31 (RTX 5070, 12 GB, busy region, 3840 × 2054): the driver's figure follows the viewer's own usage, 10.3 GB with the textures loaded and 11.2 GB once they are lowered (8.4 / 11.2 GB with a second viewer), so every 0 -> 1 step came at the low figure and every step back at the high one, the target swinging 2.7 ↔ 4.9 GB and up to 10,219 textures lowered in 40 s. Two viewers at once (6.6 and 5.9 GB) overfilled the card: the second's budget fell to 3.8 GB with its textures already at the minimum (about 4 GB of geometry, render targets and allocator room it cannot give back), GPU frames of 1–1.1 s, 1–2 fps in both, then a device lost in one. With 7 GB forced (an 8 GB card) the scene does not fit either way: the pressure climbs to step 7 within 25 s, with or without the lowering goal above. Run D (one viewer, this build, real budget): the budget given out held at 10,148 MB, but the pressure still went 0 -> 1 -> 0 every 5 to 20 s (45 to 900 textures lowered each time): the step down from 1 counted nothing taken back, while the lowering goal takes the largest textures under the level step 0 loads; the estimate one step below (`texture_budget::below_estimate`, the textures between their lowered and loaded levels) now counts from step 1 too. Run D2 (this build, one viewer, same spot): one step, 0 -> 1 eighteen seconds after the teleport, then held for the rest of the run (2 min 45 s), the pages lowered once from 5.08 to 4.36 GB and steady at 4.55 GB, the budget given out steady, 30 fps (GPU-bound), no error. ⬜ QA: a busy region on a card of 8 GB or less (or a laptop GPU): the pressure climbs to the step the scene needs and holds it; the reporters of #1557 and #1713 to confirm on the next release.

  - ✅ **2. Attachments placed on the GPU.** Largest item of the main thread in the measurement: `sync` 1.3 ms per frame, ~1,850 objects repositioned per frame (`synced`), 490 KB of records and 725 KB of journal sent per frame.
    - ✅ what avatars wear is placed by the GPU (`scene/anchors.rs`): each bone palette ends with anchors, rigid world matrices written every frame — the first places the skeleton, the following ones the attachment points of the body as they are posed (47 points, 208 matrices per skeleton instead of 192). The record of an attached prim holds its placement relative to the anchor of its point; that of a rigged mesh (attached mesh, bento, animesh attached or on the ground) and of an avatar's body reads the anchor of its skeleton instead of holding its matrix. The vertex shaders compose them (objects, prepass, shadows, reflections, impostors). GPU culling: a compute pass computes the world sphere of each object before the faces are sorted — that of an attached prim follows its anchor, that of a rigged mesh encloses the per-bone boxes of its geometry posed by the palette, as the sync did (`animesh::posed_bounds`), with the extent of the skeleton as a fallback. The sync now writes only the anchors in use (sent with the posed palettes) and no longer visits these objects as long as only their wearer moves or animates; they are repositioned when they themselves, or an object between them and their attachment point, change (script, edit, detach), and at their turn in the LOD slice. The centre of anchored objects is still kept up to date for the CPU (sorting of transparent faces, hover, lights, impostors); the lists the CPU still builds test a rigged mesh with the extent of its skeleton, like LL (a few more transparent faces drawn off screen, deliberate difference). Left to the sync as before: HUDs, flexible prims, objects that rotate or move by themselves and whatever is linked to them. Same position as before (the CPU computation and the anchors share `attach_frame` and `skeleton_model`); `AURORA_CPU_ATTACH=1` keeps the old path for comparison. What the sync visited although nothing had changed: the LOD slice, each object every 24 frames whatever the fps (24,880 / 24 ≈ 1,040 objects per frame, 60% of the visits); the HUDs of our avatar, repositioned every frame along with whatever follows its wearer (256 prims in the measured session, according to its log); the rest (avatars, flexible or rotating prims and whatever is linked to them) is not broken down in the measurement. Fixed: (1) event-driven level-of-detail checks (`scene/lod_watch.rs`) — each check leaves the still object with the distance the camera can still travel before `lod_for` can change level (`lod_slack`, inverse of `lod_for` rounded down), and the object is only checked again once the camera has travelled it: never with a still camera, a few objects per frame when it moves (those close to a change of level), all of them within 24 frames at most after a camera jump or a settings change (LOD factor, field of view); the check is still the sync's own, so same levels at the same distances, and without waiting for the object's turn; what the GPU places from an avatar (attachments, rigged meshes) moves with it and is still checked in rotation, every 24 frames while the camera moves (as before) and every 0.4 s with a still camera (the period of the slice at 60 fps, which a higher fps no longer shortens); every object is still checked every 10 s (safety net); never more checks per frame than the slice made; (2) an attached HUD no longer follows its wearer in the sync: it is repositioned on its updates and when its place on screen changes without an update (window resized, local zoom or offset), while a HUD prim that rotates by itself and whatever is linked to it are still repositioned every frame;   - ⬜ **3. Hitches when objects arrive and worst frames.** Worst frame of each second, median: `sync` 3.6 ms (14 ms at worst), `s_sync_apply` 2.0, `params` 1.5, `s_sync_plan` 1.45, `lists` 1.3.
    - ✅ parallel loops of the frame without waiting for the pool (`frame_par.rs`): the sync placement, the draw lists, the poses and the flexible prims went through a rayon `par_iter`, of which the main thread is not a worker: it slept until the end of the loop, behind the wake-up of a worker and then its own (the spikes of `s_sync_plan`, `lists` and `poses`, up to 9 ms in quiet seconds on Agni). It now starts the loop right away, in chunks taken one at a time; 1 to 7 workers join it if they wake up in time, depending on the amount of work (`Grain`), those that arrive too late are not waited for, and a short loop (lists with GPU culling, poses of a few avatars) stays on the main thread. Ruled out by measurement: everything in series (placement of 2,400 objects 0.5 → 1.0 ms on average), the main thread as a worker of the rayon pool (`use_current_thread`: worse, it falls asleep in rayon's wait), yielding its core while waiting for a helper (the system gives it to the decoding tasks). In the same PR: skeletons at rest redone every 2 to 3 s depending on the avatar, and no longer all in the same frame every 2 s (40 avatars: `poses` at 1 ms or more in one second out of two); objects waiting for geometry polled in shares beyond 2,048 (all of them within 4 frames at most; 12,000 waiting after a teleport cost 1.3 ms per frame in `s_sync_list`); the render thread finishes the scene encoder itself, the longest one, instead of waiting for it from one of its auxiliary threads. Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=3000` with `AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=40`, dev profile, shared and loaded PC: old and new code alternated every second within the same session, worst frame of each second): while objects arrive, `s_sync_plan` 1.8 → 1.2 ms median and 25.6 → 1.5 ms at the 90th percentile, `lists` 0.32 → 0.09 ms on average and 10.5 → under 1 ms at the 90th percentile, `poses` 2.6 → under 1 ms median and 31 → 1.4 ms at the 90th percentile, `sync` 26.6 → 3.6 ms at the 90th percentile, 200 → 260 fps; when quiet, `s_sync_plan` 0.48 → 0.39 ms on average and at 1 ms or more in 32 → 2% of seconds, `lists` 0.29 → 0.12 ms, `poses` 0.35 → 0.25 ms, `r_finish` 0.56 → 0.51 ms (1.9 → 1.6 ms in the worst frame of each second). Left: a helper that loses its core in the middle of a chunk is waited for (the loop borrows the main thread's data); `Scene::edit_ray_hits` (mouse wheel in edit mode) and the inventory keep `par_iter`. Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (BackBone Main Store, 16,000 to 18,200 objects, two round trips by teleport: attachments, avatars, flexible prims and arrivals correct). Compared with the previous session at the same place (same base, different crowd: order of magnitude): `s_sync_plan` 0.94 → 0.61 ms on average and at 1 ms or more in 97 → 35% of seconds, `lists` 0.61 → 0.46 ms and 15.3 → 4.2 ms at worst, `sync` 1.56 → 1.10 ms on average and 2.06 → 1.69 ms in the worst frame of each second; the remaining `s_sync_apply` of 8 to 10 ms fall on teleports (8 ms budget behind the teleport screen)
    - ✅ arrival frame of thousands of objects at once (12,000 in one go in demo, outside the loading screen: `sync` ~8.5 ms in dev profile, ~5 ms in release — all the new objects went in the same frame through the list, the parallel placement and then their first sync, and the budget of full syncs rose from 1 to 3 ms right after a long frame, hence in that very one). Fixed: a new object has nothing on screen to keep in place; it no longer goes through the frame's list or through placement, and waits for its first sync in a queue served in arrival order (`Arrivals`, `scene/sync_sets.rs`), on the time budget of full syncs: half of that budget at most while other objects are waiting for their faces, whatever is left of it afterwards. The `ObjectStore` marks new objects until their first sync (except avatars, never delayed), which avoids reading every object to recognise them; a waiting object is not visited by the LOD slice and, when listed with its parent, keeps its turn. Frame budgets (full syncs, task results, texture uploads) computed on the shorter of the last two frames: an isolated long frame no longer earns a triple budget for the next one. Table of the scene's objects written once at startup (its pages were only handed over by the system on the first write: 0.4 ms in the frame that filled it for 12,000 objects). `sync_backlog` also counts the new objects waiting. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=12000,12000`, old and new path in the same binary, alternated passes, medians (shared PC) — release, 5 passes: `sync` of the arrival frame 5.05 → 1.65 ms (modified objects and list 0.58 → 0.08, placement 1.15 → 0.04, first syncs 2.52 ms for a budget of 2.3 → 1.0 ms for a budget of 1), `sync` at worst in the 6 seconds of loading 5.09 → 2.36 ms, syncs finished 0.26 → 0.34 s after the arrival (the first syncs take 3 or 4 frames); dev profile, 4 passes: 8.25 → 2.75 ms. Screenshots identical by both paths apart from particles and clock (stream of 12,000 objects, standard demo, crowd + animesh, texture turnover, region left), GPU validation with no error; with 12,000 textures the texture memory budget kicks in in most runs on this shared GPU, with the old path as with the new one, and then leaves flat textures in this scenario. Tests: arrival queue (order, removal, slot reused), LOD slice, budget reserve, mark of new objects in the store. Limit: the first syncs follow arrival order and not distance (all done within a few frames; the faces themselves are still served from nearest to farthest).     - ✅ `r_finish`: 2.0 ms in the worst frame of each second of the measurement (3 ms at worst) for 0.55 ms on average. Cause: the filtering of the reflection probes, and not the captured face. As soon as a probe has a slot, one face is captured every frame, and the frame of the sixth face chained the filtering of the cube (mip chain, GGX radiance, irradiance) in 90 render passes, one per face and per mip; wgpu pays for each pass in `CommandEncoder::finish`. Measured by finishing the three encoders of the frame one after the other: the one for shadows, prepass and reflections takes 0.24 ms in a frame that carries only a face, and 0.98 ms (1.66 at the 95th percentile) in one frame out of six. Fixed: filtering in compute (`aurora-render/src/probes.rs`, `shaders/probe_filter.wgsl`), a single pass, one dispatch per mip for its six faces (15 dispatches), the size of the written mip giving the roughness; same computation per texel, output identical to the bit (the two filterings compared on the GPU before removing the passes: no differing component out of 530,400, radiance of the 7 mips and irradiance). The two leads noted here were not kept: the face alone does not weigh in `finish`, and a separate encoder would have kept the millisecond of filtering, on another thread. Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=40`, dev profile, shared PC: old and new filtering alternated every second within the same session, 66 s): `r_finish` 0.31 → 0.23 ms on average; in the worst frame of each second 1.19 → 0.54 ms median and 1.81 → 0.69 ms at the 90th percentile; at 1 ms or more in 20 seconds out of 22 → in none out of 44. At 120 fps (`AURORA_FPS_LIMIT=120`, same alternation, 70 s): worst frame of each second 1.85 → 0.67 ms median and 2.40 → 0.92 ms at the 90th percentile, at 1 ms or more in 22 seconds out of 23 → 4 out of 47; GPU time with no measurable change (1.45 → 1.27 ms median, `g_effects` 0.38 → 0.29 ms, within the noise of the shared card). Screenshots of the demo and of `AURORA_DEMO_PBR_OVERRIDE=1`: old / new differences within those of two screenshots of the same code (particles, clock), reflections of the shiny torus identical; `AURORA_GPU_VALIDATION=1` with no wgpu error. Tests: constants repeated by the shader, and a GPU test (`cargo test -p aurora-render probe_filter -- --ignored`: all the texels of all the mips of the slot written, each face in its layer, neighbouring slots intact). To verify on Agni (BackBone Main Store): `r_finish` absent from `max:` or clearly under 2 ms, reflections of shiny and PBR surfaces unchanged — validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12, at KB and not at the BackBone (~21,000 objects, 134 s once in the region, dev build): reflections judged good, no wgpu error in the log; in the 53 seconds where nothing loads any more, `r_finish` 0.48 ms on average, under 1 ms in 42 seconds and between 1.0 and 1.36 ms in the other 11 (2.0 ms median at the BackBone before; the comparison at the same place remains to be done at the next BackBone measurement)

(1) `between` and `rt_idle` alone at the top of `max:`: a mouse button held on the window frame (close button, title bar). Windows tracks the press in its own loop and the viewer produces no frame for as long as it lasts: neither alt-tab nor viewer work, nothing to fix. Reproduced in demo with real inputs (press of 104 / 126 / 281 ms → `between` 80 / 120 / 269 ms; alt-tab there and back: 3 ms); in the 11 profiled sessions of 2026-10-12 it falls 0 to 4 s before the exit (the click on the close button), and is only written since the quit confirmation window (before, the viewer quit before the line of the second). (2) `events` 30 to 82 ms once per session, at the login response, behind the loading screen: the inventory cache read and decoded on the main thread (3.7 MB, 6,500 items: 27 ms on an idle PC, of which 14 ms of LLSD decoding). Fixed: file, decoding and order of the items of each folder in a thread (`inventory::read_cache`); the main thread now only stores the result (`apply_cache`: 1.6 ms on the same file). Folder requests wait for the end of the read (`hold_requests`), so as not to download what the cache contains; an item that arrived in the meantime wins over the cache and its folder is downloaded. Log: "inventory cache: N folders up to date (read in … ms off the main thread, applied in … ms)". Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (login, full inventory, nothing to report): 560 folders taken from the cache, read in 30 ms in the thread and stored in 1.6 ms, `events` 6.7 ms at worst in the second of the login
    - ✅ frames while Windows holds the window (`window_hold.rs`; cause (1) of the line above, reported in use on 2026-10-13 as the viewer freezing while the mouse button stays pressed on its title bar): a mouse button pressed on the title bar, a border or the close / maximize / minimize button, a move, a resize and the system menu are followed by Windows in a message loop of its own, inside the handling of the message that started it. winit's loop does not turn meanwhile, `about_to_wait` is not called, and the redraw it asks for every frame never comes: no frame for the whole hold. Asking for the next redraw from the frame itself was tried first and is not enough: it brings the frames back for the title bar and the borders, not for the three buttons (their loop reads mouse messages only, no paint message reaches the window) nor for the system menu. All those loops deliver the messages sent from another thread: the window procedure is hooked to know when a hold begins and ends (`WM_NCLBUTTONDOWN`, a move / resize system command, `WM_ENTERMENULOOP` / `WM_EXITMENULOOP`), and for as long as it lasts a helper thread asks for an immediate repaint (`RedrawWindow` with `RDW_UPDATENOW`), which winit turns into a `RedrawRequested` on the main thread as for any frame. Outside a hold the helper sleeps and the loop is unchanged. `AURORA_WINDOW_HOLD=0` turns it off. The main thread has to stay free for Windows' loop, which handles one mouse message between two frames: with frames following one another (and the frame limiter waiting on the main thread), the human saw the dragged window lag far behind the cursor, 250 to 500 px behind a cursor moved 600 px in 0.6 s in 1 ms steps, and still there 300 ms after it stopped. So during a hold the limiter does not wait on the main thread (`window_hold::paces`): the helper waits instead between two requests, and while the cursor moves it spaces the frames out (`pause`: the main thread draws one fifth of the time at most, and not more often than every 16 ms). Demo, real mouse input, off and on in the same binary, 120 fps cap, holds of 1.5 s, worst frame of the second: title bar pressed 1,505 → 27 ms, window dragged then held 3,395 → 19, close button 1,638 → 17, minimize 1,611 → 17, maximize 1,609 → 18, left border 1,496 → 17, system menu left open 1,512 → 31, resize by the left border 1,525 → 25; about 117 fps while the button is held still (120 outside a hold), 58 or so while the cursor moves. The dragged or resized window trails the cursor by 3 to 7 px on average, as with the helper off (3 to 5). At a 500 fps cap the rate holds through the still holds. The buttons still act when released on them (maximize, close: the quit confirmation opens) and not when released elsewhere. `pause` is unit-tested; the rest takes a real window and real input. Validated by the human on 2026-10-13, on the login screen and in world (title bar held, window moved and resized, maximized then restored, which the synthetic click of the measurement script could not do, helper off or on): in the log of that session no frame over 28 ms during the holds, at 700 to 900 fps before them

The startup window is now shown once, already maximized, then asked to come to the foreground and take the focus, under Windows' rules like LLWindowWin32::show; winit's flags follow, visible first (`window_show.rs`). Same launch in demo after: foreground and focus ours as soon as it is shown, `Focused(true)` at the second frame. ⬜ To verify by the human: launches with the window maximized and restored, from the shortcut and from `aurora-tools.cmd`, and once switching to another application during the start (that one must keep the focus, the taskbar button flashes).

    - ✅ hitch on every click on the world (release session of 2026-10-12 on the grid, ~24,900 objects, SMAA, GPU-bound: a frame of 23 to 26 ms instead of 6 on every click, `between` 16 to 20 ms in `max:` and 17 ms in `off_cpu:`). Cause, reproduced in demo: a click read the depth under its pixel while waiting for the GPU (`Renderer::pick_world`) — the frame in progress on the render thread, then everything the GPU had queued (blocking `device.poll`), i.e. about three frames when the GPU is the bottleneck. Fixed: the click requests that depth and returns (`Renderer::request_pick`); the request leaves in the packet of the next frame, the render thread copies the texel before encoding that frame (depth and camera are still those of the frame on which the click was made: it is the answer of the old read, to the bit) in commands submitted separately, and the answer comes back with a frame result (`aurora-render/src/pick.rs`). The click is then resumed from its start with the answer, the cursor and the keys it had (`app/click_pick.rs`): left click, Alt + click, right click, build tools and Focus tool go through this same path, their search for the object and the point unchanged. Like Firestorm's `pickAsync` and `delayInputProcessing` (camera, building), whatever follows a pending click — its release, the other buttons, the mouse movement that moves the camera — waits behind it, in order: nothing is lost. Accepted difference: the action of a click starts 3 frames later when the GPU is the bottleneck (roughly the time the wait used to last), 1 or 2 with an fps cap, where the old read only waited 0.6 to 2 ms (answer in 8.3 ms median at 120 fps, 16.7 ms at 60, 67 ms at 30; the result of a frame already finished by the render thread is taken at the start of the next frame, without waiting for its presentation); a camera transition starts that much later and ends at the same place. Demo (`AURORA_DEMO_CLICKS=250`: 4 clicks per second on the ground; `AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=250`, `AURORA_DEMO_ANIMESH=1`, `AURORA_MAX_AVATARS=300`, `AURORA_AA=6`: 14,562 objects, 255 posed skeletons; dev profile, shared PC, old and new read alternated every second within the same process, 4 passes of 80 to 100 s during which the GPU load from other programs varied: 186, 75, 42 and 32 fps): `between` in the worst frame of the second, median, 8.2 / 42.9 / 73.3 / 95.2 ms → 1.3 / 2.3 / 1.6 / 1.6 ms; worst frame of the second 13.8 / 50.9 / 79.3 / 101.2 ms → 6.9 / 17.0 / 28.7 / 34.5 ms; the wait of a click was 6.4 / 25.7 / 66.2 / 90.3 ms, its answer now arrives after 2 frames (GPU free, no fps cap) or 3 (GPU-bound), i.e. 10.8 / 35.5 / 67.8 / 91.6 ms. Check `AURORA_CLICK_PICK=check` (both reads done and compared on every click; `wait`: the old one alone): 4,736 clicks swept over the whole window (`AURORA_DEMO_CLICKS=100,sweep,<kind>`), the five kinds of click, MSAA and SMAA, with and without render thread, with and without fps cap, crowd and 9,000 cubes: same depth and same target on every click. 552 clicks released before their answer (50 ms frames): all finished cleanly. 30 existing demo scenarios (click actions, menus, Alt camera, steering, building, HUDs) replayed with the old then the new read: same log lines, apart from the intermediate frames of a camera transition (about fifteen centimetres of difference during a transition, 1 cm on arrival). Validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (KB, dev build, ~28,600 objects, 68 posed skeletons, 66 clicks in three minutes: "perfect"). Measurement of that session: answer in 2 to 4 frames (20.8 ms on average, 36 ms at worst); in the 58 seconds that carry a click, `between` is 2.4 ms median in `max:` and 5.0 ms at worst, instead of 16 to 20 ms

    - ✅ measured then fixed. Measurement: `params` is split in the profile (`p_*`: `screen`, `env`, `mirror`, `part_sources`, `part_sim`, `part_list`, `lights`, `probes`, see docs/TESTING.md) and the demo has a particle load (`AURORA_DEMO_PARTICLES=load`, 32 fountains, ~4,000 particles). Demo `AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=12000,400` + `AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=40` + `AURORA_DEMO_PARTICLES=load` (14,369 objects, 41 avatars, 3,990 particles), dev build: of the 0.31 ms of `params`, the particles take 0.26 (84%) — 0.08 to collect the systems set by updates, by a walk over all objects, 0.07 of simulation, 0.11 for the sorted list — then the mirror 0.03 (walk over all the objects of the scene), the probes 0.02; environment, lights and loading screen do not count. The spikes come mostly from that walk: in a 25 s measurement on the loaded PC (without the particle load), `p_part_sources` reaches 1 ms in 16% of seconds and 4.9 ms at worst (it reads the whole memory of the objects), and only one other part gets there, once (`p_part_sim`, 1.5 ms). Fixed: the `ObjectStore` keeps two more streams (`take_particle_changes`, `take_sound_changes`) noted by full updates, read instead of the walks by `ParticleManager::update` and by `App::flush_object_sounds` (the latter also ran before each sound message; the full walk only remains when the block list changes); mirrors are listed by the sync like lights (`Scene::mirror_objects`); the orientation of bodies (`World::update_bodies`) and loading avatars (`Scene::update_loading`) read the `ObjectStore`'s list of avatars. `extras` came mostly from elsewhere: for each avatar, every frame, the texture of each face of everything it wears was looked up to be requested with priority, including once the avatar is displayed, when the result is not used; this is now done only while it is a cloud, and the state of an attached mesh is only consulted if it is pending. Particles: the back-to-front order is sorted on 8-byte integers (distance then rank, hence stable from one frame to the next at equal distance) instead of the 48-byte instances. Same rules and same processing order as before (same seeds of the particle sources).
